FUNCTIONS AND ACTIVITIES ENVIRONMENTAL DATA SERV 

ICE. This service operates data centers, such as the National Weather 

Records Center at Asheville, N.C., for the storage, retrieval, compilation, publication, and dissemination of environmental data for use by commerce, industry, the scientific and engineering community, and the general public. It conducts research to improve the quality and availability of environmental data, to insure its widest and best use; and it coordinates climatological and geophysical data matters with world scientific organizations. 

WEATHER BUREAU.-The Weather 

Bureau provides the national weather service. It observes and reports the weather of the United States and its possessions and develops and distributes forecasts of weather conditions and warnings of severe storms, floods, and other adverse weather conditions. 

The Bureau participates in international meteorological and hydrological activities, and provides forecasts for domestic and international aviation and for shipping on the high seas. Performance of these functions includes the operation of a natonal network of field offices and forecast centers. [For regulations codified under Weather Bureau, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 15, Chapter V] INSTITUTES FOR ENVIRONMENTAL RESEARCH.-The Institutes conduct an integrated research program relating to the oceans and inland waters, the lower and upper atmosphere, the space environment and the earth to increase understanding of man's environment in order to provide more useful services; and conduct propagation research and services in support of the Nation's telecommunication activities. 

Certain observatories and laboratories and operated in the field where necessary to observe environmental phenomena.

COAST AND GEODETIC SURVEY.-The 

Coast and Geodetic Survey provides: charts for marine and air navigation, a basic network of geodetic control, and other basic data for engineering, scientific, commercial, industrial, and defense needs. In performance of these functions it conducts surveys, investigations, analyses, and research in the following fields: hydrography, oceanography, geodesy, cartography, photogrammetry, geomagnetism, seismology, gravity, and astronomy. It directs certain field operations including field offices, mobile survey parties, observatories, and ocean survey vessels. It also operates a seismic sea wave warning system to alert Pacific coastal intersts of sudden and destructive tidal waves. NATIONAL ENVIRONMENTAL SATEL- LITE CENTER.The Center manages and coordinates all operational satellite programs within the Environmental 

Science Services Administration and operates satellite systems for the acquisition of environmental data. It conducts research in new applications and methods of acquiring environmental data through satellites, and also conducts research in satellite instrumentation, satellite orbits and observational techniques, satellite telemetry, satel lite data recording and processing techniques, and other aspects of satellite systems engineering. The Center operates certain field installations such as Command and Data Acquisition Stations at locations required by the satellite system.

PURPOSE. The primary function assigned EDA by statute is the longrange economic development and programing for areas and regions of substantial and persistent unemploymen and underemployment and low family incomes through the creation of new employment opportunities by develop ing new and expanding existing facili ties and resources in such areas and regions.

FUNCTIONS AND ACTIVITIES COMMISSIONER.-The COMPLIANCE Compliance Commissioner conducts hearings and performs other duties with respect to administrative compliance proceedings involving export control violation cases.

ADVISORY COMMITTEE ON EXPORT POLICY (ACEP) EXECUTIVE SECRETAR- IAT. The Secretariat serves ACEP, the interdepartmental committee established under the Export Control Act to provide information and advice to the Secretary of Commerce on export licenses, policies, and programs. 

FOREIGN-TRADE ZONES BOARD EXECU- TIVE SECRETARIAT.-This unit conducts regulatory, administrative, and techni cal affairs of the Foreign-Trade Zones 

Board, as required by the Foreign- 

Trade Zones Act (19 U.S.C. 81a-81u) 

which provides for the establishment, operation, and maintenance of foreigntrade zones in or adjacent to ports of entry of the United States.

The zones are approved sites where foreign and domestic merchandise may be brought without being subject to U.S. customs laws governing entry or payment of duties. Facilities are available to foreign as well as American business firms. They afford advantages to firms engaged in manufacturing, export, re-export, import, and transshipment.

Six zones and two industrial subzones are operated currently in New 

York, Louisiana, California, Washington, Ohio, and Puerto Rico. A new general-purpose zone is now being established in Honolulu, Hawaii.

Maritime Administration was established by Reorganization Plan 21 of 

1950, effective May 24, 1950, as one of the successor agencies to the former 

United States Maritime Commission.

PURPOSE. The Maritime Adminis tration administers programs authorized by the Merchant Marine Act, 1936, as amended, and related shipping statutes to aid in the development, promotion, and operation of the U.S. merchant marine, so that it will be (a) adequate to carry the Nation's domestic waterborne commerce and a substantial portion of its foreign commerce during peacetime; (b) capable of serving as a naval and military auxiliary in time of war or national emergency; (c) owned and operated under U.S. flag by citizens of the United States, so far as may be practicable; and (d) composed of the best equipped, safest, and most suitable types of ships manned by a trained and efficient citizen personnel.

ORGANIZATION.-The Maritime Ad ministration is headed by a Maritime Administrator, who is appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate. Its headquarters organization in Washington,

D.C., is composed of an Office of Pre gram Planning, Office of Budget an Management, Office of Public Infor mation, Office of Statistics, Office o 

Personnel Management, Office of th General Counsel, Office of the Comp troller, Office of Property and Supply Office of Ship Construction, Office Research and Development, Office 

Ship Operations, and Office of Gov ernment Aid. 

There is established within th 

Maritime Administration a Maritim 

Subsidy Board, composed of the Mar time Administrator, who serves a 

Chairman, the Deputy Maritime Ac ministrator, and the General Counse each of whom acts pursuant to direc authority from the Secretary of Com merce. The Board makes, amends, an terminates contracts for operating-di ferential and construction-differentia subsidies. It conducts hearings an makes determinations antecedent t these actions; and it investigates an determines the relative costs of con structing ships in the United State and in foreign countries and of oper ating ships under United States and competitive foreign flags.

The Maritime Administrator is als vested with the residual powers and

In the districts, the Offices of the tlantic, Gulf, and Pacific Coast Dictors located at New York, N.Y., ew Orleans, La., and San Francisco, alif., are responsible for all field ofces and programs of the Maritime dministration within their respective past areas, except ship construction nd maritime training. 

FUNCTIONS AND ACTIVITIES GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE TO SHIP- ING.-The Maritime Administration dministers the operating-differential nd construction-differential subsidy rograms and other Government aids o merchant shipping, authorized by w. Under these programs, the Govrnment pays the difference between ertain costs of operating ships under S.-flag and foreign competitive flags, n essential foreign trade routes; and e difference (not to exceed a certain ercent of the total cost) between the osts of constructing ships in the Inited States and in foreign shipuilding centers. The Administration also investicates and determines ocean services, outes, and lines essential for the deelopment and maintenance of the oreign commerce of the United

The Administration assists the shipping industry to generate increased trade and cargo shipments for U.S.-flag ships. Shippers, freight forwarders, and manufacturers are encouraged to use U.S.-flag shipping in conformance with sections 101 and 212(d) of the act of 1936, as an aid to the U.S. merchant marine, and to assist in developing a credit position in balance of payments.

RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT.- The Maritime Administration con ducts research and development activities in the maritime field, including cargo handling, development and utilization of new ship designs, marine transportation systems, transportation systems, advanced propulsion concepts, and ship mechanization and management techniques. The objectives of this program are to improve the efficiency and economy of operations of the American merchant marine and to promote more rapid technical advancement of it. 

SHIPBUILDING AND DESIGN. .-The Maritime Administration develops plans and specifications for prototype ships. It encourages and participates in the development of plans and designs by subsidized operators under their ship replacement programs, and by applicants for Government aid covering ships proposed to be constructed or converted. It inspects ships during the course of work to assure conformance with approved plans and specifications.

To carry out the national maritime policy, the Maritime Administration, with the approval of the President, constructs, reconstructs, and reconditions ships for Government account. 

The Administration is authorized to sell these ships, charter them to private operators, or utilize them for Government operation.

SHIP OPERATIONS AND REPAIR. 

The Maritime Administration charters 

Government-owned ships to United States operators when it is determined that such charters will promote the national maritime policy. During national emergencies it requisitions or procures for operation or for charter ships owned by citizens of the United States or under construction, and it determines requirements for and allocates ships to meet the needs of national defense programs. In connection with the foregoing the Maritime Administration prescribes ship operations and ship repair standards and administers such standards under the provisions of charter and general agency agreements and operatingdifferential subsidy contracts. 

NATIONAL DEFENSE RESERVE FLEET.-The Maritime Administra tion maintains national defense reserve fleets of Government-owned ships determined by the Maritime Administration and the Department of Defense to be essential for national defense. It sells or otherwise disposes of ships determined to be nonessential for national defense purposes.

OPERATION OF WAREHOUSES.-The Maritime Administration maintains and operates four warehouses for the storage of marine equipment required for the reactivation, repair, and operation of ships.

MARITIME TRAINING.-The Maritime Administration operates the U. S. 

Merchant Marine Academy, Kings 

Point, N. Y. Academy graduates are licensed as merchant marine officers and qualified for commissions as en signs in the U. S. Naval Reserve. The 

Administration also administers grant-in-aid program for the five maritime academies operated by five

States: California, Maine, Massachu setts, New York, and Texas. 

CONSTRUCTION RESERVE FUNDS.- 

Under regulations jointly issued by the 

Secretary of Commerce and the Secre tary of the Treasury, American ship owners may deposit proceeds from th sale or loss of ships and earnings from operation of ships in tax-deferre funds, for use in the construction or ad quisition of new ships. 

TRANSFER OF SHIPS TO ALIENS.- The Maritime Administration regu lates the sales to aliens, and transfer to foreign registry, of ships owned i whole or in part by citizens of th United States and documented unde the laws of the United States, and, i time of war or national emergency, o ships so owned without regard t documentation. 

WAR RISK INSURANCE.-The Mari time Administration is authorized to provide Government war risk insur ance of merchant ships, their cargoe and crews, when adequate insurance cannot be obtained on reasonable terms and conditions from private in surance companies in the United 

States.

Assistant Secretary for Manpower

The Assistant Secretary for Man power has responsibility for all the De- The Manpower Administration is composed of the offices and bureaus described in the following paragraphs. 

Manpower Administration 

Office of Manpower Policy, Evaluation and Research This office performs planning, research, and evaluation functions. It develops and recommends plans for a comprehensive national manpower program that will guide and make possible the coordination of decisions and activities of the Department of Labor, and in addition provide guidelines for other Federal agencies, employers, labor unions, professional organizations, State and local governments (including those engaged in educational activity), private educational institutions, and others in making and executing manpower decisions. This includes the development of policies and standards. for implementing such manpower development and utilization programs as enumerated above. and the interdepartmental and intradepartmental committee activities of the Department, the Assistant to the 

Under Secretary (Field Operations), and the Department's historical research activities.

The Office appraises the manpower requirements and resources of the Nation and develops policies, objectives, and standards to deal with the problems of persistent and other types of unemployment and underemployment, while considering such factors as current and prospective manpower shortages, dislocations in the economy arising from automation or other technological developments, foreign competition, relocation of industry, shifts nx partment manpower programs and activities. in market demands, and other changes in the structure of the economy. 

The Office provides leadership in planning, evaluating, and coordinating the manpower and automation research and related statistic programs in the Department and identifies the need for and plans, conducts, or arranges for other bureaus of the Department or other Government or private agencies to conduct high-priority, pathfinding research to augment existing research in the manpower area. The objective is to identify the many ramifications and the dimensions of the manpower problems of the Nation and to seek through research, adequate solutions to these problems. It plans and directs developmental and experimental stud ies in all areas of manpower and automation to find solutions to problems which significantly affect the Nation's ability to eliminate persistent and other types of unemployment and underem ployment and to evaluate the impact of and benefits and problems created by automation and other forms of technological progress. It plans and develops a program to increase and expand knowledge of how occupational unemployment and underemployment competence that will aid in eliminating is achieved.

The Office prepares materials for the President's and the Secretary of

Labor's Annual Manpower Reports together with recommendations for action. It prepares the Secretary of 

Labor's annual report to the Congress

It maintains a clearinghouse of technical and research information on manpower, automation, and training.

The Bureau of Apprenticeship and Training carries out the objectives of the act in conformance with policies determined by the Federal Committee on Apprenticeship, an 11-member committee appointed by the Secretary of Labor and composed of 5 representatives each from management and labor and 1 from the U.S. Office of 

Education. 

The Bureau promotes the establishment and improvement of apprenticeship and other on-the-job training programs and provides technical assistance and training aids where necessary. Its functions are to aid management and labor in recognizing the need for apprenticeship. Through field representatives in each State the Bureau works closely with employers, labor, vocational schools, and others concerned with apprenticeship programs throughout industry. Programs must meet standards established by the Federal Committee on Apprenticeship to be registered with the Bureau.

The Bureau has responsibility for on-the-job training under the Man power Development and Training 

Act. Agreements are made with employers, labor unions, associations, and public agencies to conduct training programs using the facilities of such groups to train the unemployed, underemployed, and those whose skills. have become or are becoming obsolete. On-the-job training under this program may be combined with supplemental technical instruction by agreement with public schools. 

Bureau of Employment Security 

[For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 20, Chapter V] 

The Bureau's responsibilities are related to the administration of a nationwide system of public employment services, State unemployment insurance programs, Federal unemployment compensation programs, and special manpower programs designed to relieve the effects of unemployment and to promote maximum utilization of the Nation's manpower. The legisla tive bases for the Bureau's operations include the Wagner-Peyser Act, the 

Federal Unemployment Tax Act, titles III, IX, XII, and XV of the Social Security Act, the Farm Labor Contrac tor Registration Act, various provi sions in the Immigration and Nationality Act, the Automotive Products, Trade Act, the Public Works and Economic Development Act, the Manpower Development and Training Act, the Vocational Education Act of 1963, the Trade Expansion Act, the Eco nomic Opportunity Act, and the Civil 

Rights Act. 

The Bureau coordinates employment security activities with other Govern ment agencies and the public, and advises the legislative and executive branches on employment security matters. It plans programs on a nationwide basis. To facilitate sound program planning, it collects and analyzes operational and economic data related to employment security programs, which in published form provide Government, labor, management, and the public with information of value in assessing economic trends and developments.

The Bureau conducts evaluations of the administration and operation of 

State employment security agencies.

This involves the measurement of achievements, the making of recom mendations for improving State administrative operations and management, and the provision of assistance in the establishment of improved methods of administration and operation. 

Fiscal responsibilities involve determination of funds needed and justification of appropriation requests before Congress, allocation of funds among States, establishment of standards for expenditures, auditing of State fiscal accounts and records, filing of exceptions on funds improperly expended,

JAUME  

331 review of applicable State laws and their execution, and certification of laws which meet Federal requirements to permit the allocation of Federal funds for administrative costs. 

The Bureau provides leadership to the State employment security agencies, involving responsibility to: (1) develop and interpret national policies and goals; (2) study program needs and administrative problems; (3) develop techniques, tools, and measures for improvement in administration and program content; (4) promote adoption of improvements in

State legislation and administration; and (5) provide continuing technical assistance and interchange of experience and information.

The Bureau works closely with State agencies in the development and maintenance of a well-selected and trained staff.

The Bureau coordinates nationwide developmental projects designed to provide tools, methods, and material for adaptive use throughout the employment security system. From such coordinated efforts have come such products as the Dictionary of Occupational Titles, occupational tests, and occupational job descriptions. 

The Bureau's employment service program responsibilities, as assigned to its United States Employment Service under the provisions of the Wagner- Peyser Act, include assistance in establishing and maintaining a system of public employment offices in the States and territories; assistance in coordinating the system throughout the country and increasing its usefulness by developing and prescribing minimum standards of efficiency; collecting and furnishing information as to opportunities for employment and other information of value in operating the system, including information about labor area developments by industry and occupation and classification of certain areas according to relative labor supply; maintaining a public employment service for the District of Columbia, a veterans' service devoted to securing employment for veterans, and a placement service for agriculture and its workers; and maintaining a system for interarea recruitment of labor among the States. The United States Employ ment Service guides and assists the States in placement functions, occupational analysis, counseling, and testing functions; in maximizing employment opportunities for veterans, older workers, youth, handicapped workers, members of minority groups, and workers affected by the impact of automation and changing technology; in promoting community efforts toward the greatest possible use of the labor force; in promoting use by employers of the public employment service; and in providing materials and techniques to employers for effective use of man power. The Employment Service as sists State agencies in providing a full range of services to rural areas. In many States mobile teams of counselors, interviewers, and test administrators extend these services. 

The Bureau cooperates with other offices of the Department and with other Federal agencies in the war on poverty, especially in developing employability among culturally, educationally, and economically deprived youth. It is responsible under title VI of the Civil 

Rights Act for insuring that the Federal-State employment security program is administered without discrimination on the basis of race, color, or country of origin.

The Bureau also actively participates in manpower mobilization planning and in the preparation being made by the Federal Government for national emergencies which might arise. In addition, the Bureau coordinates civil defense and mobilization activities in State employment security agencies.

The Bureau's unemployment insurance program responsibilities assigned to its Unemployment Insurance Service include review and analysis of State laws to determine if they are in conformity with the Social Security Act, the Federal Unemployment Tax Act, and regulations of the Secretary of Labor; review of State administration of unemployment insurance to determine whether the program is operating in compliance with Federal requirements, and whether individuals are denied benefits to which they are entitled under the State law and under the various agreements with the Secretary of Labor to carry out the Federal 

Unemployment Compensation programs for former Federal civilian employees and ex-servicemen; establishment of feasible criteria for measuring administrative costs for use in determining the amounts of money necessary for proper and efficient administration of the State unemployment compensation laws; and furnishing assistance to the States on administrative and operating problems, in applying or adapting improved administrative procedures developed by the Bureau or by individual States, and in developing legislative recommendations designed to improve the program under the economy of each State. The 

Bureau also analyzes past trends and forecasts future trends in coverage, contributions, benefit rights, and benefit payments State by State and in the Nation as a whole; studies and recommends methods of improving the unemployment insurance program; disseminates information on the operation of the unemployment insurance program; assists the States in conducting studies of the effect of proposed program changes as well as their current programs, and in preparing evaluations of the solvency of the 

States' unemployment insurance benefit funds, as well as of the continued adequacy of the States' reserves and tax structures in light of actual or proposed amendments to the laws and the expected future incidence of unemployment; reviews applications for advances (loans) from the Federal 

Unemployment Account, made by

Governors of States with low reserves, and certifies (for the Secretary of Labor) to the Secretary of the Treasury the amount of such advance to which the State is eligible under title XII of the Social Security Act; studies and develops policy recommendations concerning other governmental or private income-maintenance programs which may affect the unemployment insurance system; arranges with State employment security agencies for payment of training allowances under the Man power Development and Training Act, of readjustment allowances under the 

Trade Expansion Act of 1962 to work ers found by the U.S. Tariff Commission to have been affected adversely by tariff concessions under the act or to workers determined to have been adversely affected by the Automotive

Act of 1962, to workers and their fam ilies when a move to another location is necessary to obtain full-time employment; and develops plans for the emer gency payment of unemployment allowances in situations of enemy attack or national disaster. The Federal Advisory Council on

BYX Neighborhood Youth Corps 

 Regulations, Title 29, Subtitle A] The Neighborhood Youth Corps 

(NYC) is responsible for administering the work-training program for unemployed young men and women, age 16 through 21, from low-income families, authorized in title I, part B, of the 

Economic Opportunity Act of 1964 (78 

Stat. 508; 42 U.S.C. 2701).

The purpose of this part of the antipoverty program is to make it possible for young people to remain in school, For return to school if they have already left; or to provide useful work experience to increase employability and to develop good work habits for those who are unemployed and out of school. 

Enrollees in the NYC undertake useful public service types of work which would not otherwise be performed in their own home community. A broad range of work is being undertaken. Examples are the conservation, development, or management and improvement of State or community natural resources or recreational facilities, and a wide variety of assistance to teachers and administrators in the schools.

There must be no displacement of employed workers or impairment of contracts for services. Region

The fiscal 1966 budget estimate is 370,000 job opportunities for disadvantaged youths enrolled under the NYC program in all States of the Union.

NYC projects originate with local or State groups. Sponsors may be non- 

Federal public or private nonprofit organizations including States, counties, municipalities, or authorized subdivisions such as park commissions, boards of education, and libraries; or private nonprofit organizations, such as health and welfare associations, hospitals, and settlement houses. Preference is given to projects that are components of 

Community Action Programs undertaken under title II of the Economic Opportunity Act. 

The NYC functions under delega tion of authority to the Secretary of

Labor by the Director of the Office of 

Economic Opportunity and in conformity with rules and regulations jointly promulgated. The Administrator, acting for the Secretary of Labor, enters directly into agreements with approved sponsors to carry out NYC projects which are financed up to 90 percent by the Federal Government.

Labor-Management Services 

Administration 

The Labor-Management Services Administration was established by Sec retary's Order 24-63, dated August 8, 1963. The Labor-Management Serv ices Administrator is responsible for the direction and coordination of all the Department's labor-management relations programs and activities. He is assisted by a Deputy Administrator and other officials having responsibility for the specific functions of the comprehensive labor-management relations program. 

The Labor-Management Services 

Administration is composed of the offices described in the following paragraphs. 

Assistant Secretary for Labor-Management Relations and Disclosure Act of 1959 (73 Stat 

519; 29 U.S.C. 401 note) for which the Secretary of Labor has authority and responsibility.

The Welfare and Pension Plans Dis closure Act provides for the reporting and disclosure of information concerning the operation of welfare and pension plans and the bonding of persons handling such plans, provides specific power to investigate complaints and to secure compliance and restrain viola tions of the law through civil judicial proceedings, and to issue binding and authoritative opinions and interpretations.

OFFICE OF LABOR-MANAGEMENT AND WELFARE-PENSION REPORTS.-The Of fice administers and enforces the provisions of the Welfare and Pension

Plans Disclosure Act (72 Stat. 997, as amended; 29 U.S.C. 301 note), and the Labor-Management Reporting directed from seven regional, nine district, and nine field offices. Functions of field representatives are to inform State and local authorities and private nonprofit agencies about the NYC, to assist in developing suitable projects, to review proposed projects and to follow their progress, and to report on needs of youth for work experience in their regions and to cooperate with local em ployment service and Youth Opportu nity Center job placement activities. 

The Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act provides for the re porting and disclosure of certain finan cial transactions and administrative practices of labor organizations and employers; the prevention of abuses in these areas and in the administration of trusteeships by labor organizations; and the enforcement of standards and procedures with respect to the election and removal of officers of labor organizations. Both acts authorize the conduct of investigations and the initiation of civil and criminal legal actions.

Wage and Hour and Public Contracts Divisions 

[For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 29, Chapter V; Title 41, Chapter 50] The Wage and Hour Division was established pursuant to the provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act of 

June 25, 1938 (52 Stat. 1060; 29

U.S.C. 201-219). The Public Con tracts Division was created to admin ister the Walsh-Healey Public Contracts Act of June 30, 1936 (49 Stat. 

2036; 41 U.S.C. 35-45). The two Divisions were consolidated by order of the Secretary of Labor on August 21, 1942. The Wage and Hour and Public 

Contracts Divisions are headed by an Administrator, appointed by the President with the consent of the Senate. 

The Fair Labor Standards Act of 

1938, as amended, establishes, subject to specified exemptions, minimum wage, overtime compensation, and child labor standards for employees who, on an individual basis, are engaged in interstate or foreign commerce or in production of goods for commerce, including any closely reto employees of certain large enterprises engaged in commerce or the production of goods for commerce. The 

Equal Pay Act of 1963, which amended the Fair Labor Standards Act, requires employers to pay equal wages within an establishment to men and women doing equal work.

The Walsh-Healey Public Contracts 

Act requires Federal Government supply contracts in amounts exceeding $10,000 to contain stipulations with respect to payment of minimum wages and overtime, nonemployment of child and convict labor, and observance of certain safety and health standards. process or occupation directly essential thereto. The act also applies 

The McNamara-O'Hara Service 

Contract Act of 1965 extends labor standards protection to employees of contractors and subcontractors furnishing services to Federal agencies. Federal service contracts in excess of $2,500 are required to contain stipulations concerning the payment of prevailing wages and fringe benefits, and observance of safety and health standards. All employees performing work under service contracts, including contracts of $2,500 or less, must be paid at least the minimum wage provided by the Fair Labor Standards Act. 

WHPC's national office develops policies and programs, issues regulations and interpretations, conducts economic research, develops certification standards for learners, apprentices, full-time students, and handicapped workers, establishes prevailing minimum wage rates under the Public 

Contracts Act and the Service Con tract Act, coordinates the enforcement program, and directs a continuous evaluation to assure uniform and proper application of the acts. 

WHPC operates through 11 regions, each headed by a regional director who is responsible for investigation and enforcement activities in his region. Field offices and field stations operate within each region. An area office is located in Puerto Rico. In addition, safety and health investiga

Assistant Secretary for International Affairs

The Assistant Secretary for Inter national Affairs has responsibility for the Department's international activities, and for the Bureau of International Labor Affairs. He serves as the 

EU.S. Government member of the Gov erning Body of the International Labor Organization (ILO), as head of the 

U.S. delegation to the Annual Conference of the ILO, and as a member of the Board of Foreign Service. 

Bureau of International Labor Affairs 

The Bureau was established on December 31, 1959, replacing the Office of International Labor Affairs origi nally established in 1947. Under the policy direction of the Assistant Secretary of Labor for International Affairs, the Bureau is headed by an Administrator who is responsible for discharging Department of Labor functions in the international labor field. Under the policy direction of the Assistant Secretary, the Administrator is also charged with mobilizing, directing, and coordinating all other international activities of the Department's various specialized offices and bureaus. 

These functions and responsibilities of the Bureau include advising on the implications of international labor developments in relation to U.S. foreign and domestic policy, analyzing the impact of domestic policy and developments on labor aspects of foreign affairs, recommending operations designed to promote the United States national interest in the foreign labor field generally and with respect to specific areas of the world, and, with the assistance of other offices and bureaus, operating programs affecting labor which are designed to implement foreign policy.

The Bureau's staff of geographic area specialists develops detailed action programs in the field of labor for the various foreign countries. Through these country programs, the Government's efforts are coordinated to achieve U.S. foreign policy objectives as they relate to labor abroad. 

The Department of Labor has primary responsibility, under the overall foreign policy guidance of the Department of State, for United States participation in the International Labor 

Organization. 

The Bureau also carries out the Department's responsibilities for assisting the Department of State in the management of the Foreign Service, including the labor attaché and Foreign Service labor-reporting programs (the Department has statutory membership on the Board of the Foreign Service); for representation on delegations and formulation of labor policy in connection with United States participation in the United Nations Economic and Social Council and its various commissions; for participation in the 

Trade Staff Committee and other interagency trade expansion activities and for staff support for the Department's representatives on the Trade 

Expansion Act Advisory Committee and the Trade Executive Committee; for overseeing the adjustment assistance programs under the Trade Expansion Act; for assisting the Secretary in making determinations for adjustment assistance under the Automotive Products Trade Act of 1965; and for participation of labor missions in the Government's international trade fair program. In these activities the Bureau relies upon technical assistance from other bureaus of the Department. 

The Bureau coordinates and directs programs, both its own and those of other bureaus, which are carried on by the Department under various acts of Congress and under administrative agreements with other agencies for development of a fund of labor and manpower knowledge for use both in domestic and overseas programs; for development of a reservoir of labor and manpower experts (the Depart- 017

As requested, consultants are supplied for foreign assignments, technical materials are furnished for use abroad, and training programs are conducted in the United States for foreign nationals. These programs are implemented in cooperation with the Department's bureaus and regional offices, State departments of labor, American trade unions, management, and other private organizations.

Continuous research is carried on by the Bureau's technical experts to help it formulate policies and programs. 

Some studies provide information on the trends in the employment of women and on the characteristics of the female work force. Such studies point up the changes taking place and their impact on women. Other studies are concerned with employment opportunities, wages, and conditions of work in individual occupations or industries. The Bureau makes digests of existing labor laws and regulations covering women, and laws affecting women's civil and political status. It provides technical assistance to governmental and nongovernmental organizations on proposed legislation and administrative procedures. Bureau of Labor Standards 

[For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 29, Chapter XIII] 

The Bureau, established by departmental order in 1934, is a service agency to State labor departments and officials, and to labor, employer, and civic groups interested in improving working conditions. The Bureau promotes industrial safety and health, develops standards in the field of labor legislation and labor law administration, and in cooperation with the Bureau of International Labor Affairs assists in implementing international labor standards. In cooperation with the Bureau of International Labor

Affairs, it also carries on programs for international exchange of persons and training.

LEGISLATIVE AND STANDARDS.-The Bureau provides technical information and assistance to groups and individuals interested in securing adequate and well administered labor laws. Basic materials are prepared, including summaries of various types of laws and information on the effective administration of labor laws covering a broad field of labor standards. Staff members give technical assistance to State labor departments, management, labor organizations, and civic groups on labor legislation and administration, and in adapting recommended standards and procedures to meet State needs. Governments, international agencies, and interested groups of other countries are provided information on labor law and its administration in this country.

The Employees' Compensation Ap peals Board was established in the Federal Security Agency by Reorganiza tion Plan 2, effective July 16, 1946. Re organization Plan 19, effective May 24 1950, provided for the transfer of the Board and its functions to the Depart ment of Labor. The Board consists of three members appointed by the Secretary of Labor, one of whom is designated as chairman and administrative officer. The func tion of the Board is to consider and decide appeals from final decisions of the Director, Bureau of Employees 

Compensation, and of the Governor of

the Canal Zone in cases arising under the Federal Employees' Compensation Act (5 U.S.C. 751). (For coverage of the Federal Employees' Compensation 

Act, see Bureau of Employees' Compensation.) Appeals may be taken to the Board on disputed questions of law and facts, and on the basis of abuse or failure to exercise discretion.

An appeal may be filed pursuant to the Board's rules of procedure which may be found in title 20 of the Code of Federal Regulations, Part 501. Ap plication for review forms may be

Bureau of Labor Statistics 

The Bureau of Labor, the predeces sor of the Bureau of Labor Statistics, was established in the Department of the Interior, by act of June 27, 1884.

In 1913, after several changes in status, it became the Bureau of Labor Statisics in the newly created Department of Labor. The Bureau is the Govern ment's principal factfinding agency in the field of labor economics, particularly with respect to the collection and analysis of data on employment and manpower, productivity and technological developments, wages, indusrial relations, work injuries, prices, and costs and standards of living. 

The Bureau has no enforcement or administrative functions. Practically all of the basic data it collects from workers, businessmen, and from other governmental agencies are supplied by voluntary cooperation based on their nterest in and need for the analyses and summaries which result. The reearch and statistical projects planned by the Bureau grow out of the needs of these groups, as well as the needs of Congress and the Federal and State governments. The information colobtained from the Board, but informal applications which set forth grounds of the appeal are also acceptable. 

New evidence may not be submitted to the Board; its review is limited to the evidence in the case record. The appeals procedure includes, upon request, a hearing for the presentation of oral argument. In cases reviewed upon the merits, the decision contains a written opinion setting forth the reasons for action taken. The decisions of the 

Board are final. of 

ECONOMIC GROWTH.-' -The Bureau performs research and coordinating functions in relation to the program work on economic growth and employment opportunities, utilizing a wide range of data including the effects of trends in population, labor force, employment, productivity, interindustry relationship, pattern of consumer expenditures investment, Government expenditures, foreign trade, etc., on various economic models and projections.

Labor Statistics lected is issued in special bulletins and in its official publication, the Monthly 

Labor Review. 

EMPLOYMENT AND THE LABOR 

FORCE. Data are published each month on the labor force, employment, and unemployment, by age, sex, occupation, etc., based on a sample survey of the population. At recurring intervals the surveys provide estimates of the educational attainment of the labor force, the employment of students, family relationship of workers, and other personal and economic characteristics of the labor force. 

National estimates are published each month on the employment of wage and salary workers in 401 manufacturing and nonmanufacturing industries. National labor turnover rates are provided for 224 industries in manufacturing, mining, and communications. In cooperation with State

Comprehensive analyses, together with all the Government's current statistics on labor force, employment, and unemployment are published monthly in Employment and

Earnings and Monthly Report on the 

Labor Force. 

The Bureau conducts studies of trends in unemployment, of problems affecting particular groups in the working population, such as youth and older workers, and prepares analyses and projections of the changing size and composition of the labor force. In addition, the Bureau is responsible for assessment of the military manpower pool and for projections of potential manpower resources, in relation to requirements under conditions of national emergency.

Exploratory research is now being undertaken looking toward the development of a national system of statistics on job vacancies. Such data will contribute greatly to the improvement of knowledge about the Nation's labor markets and will be useful in interpreting trends in the levels of unemployment and the requirements for manpower development and retraining. 

Developmental research is being conducted in additional areas pursuant to the recommendations of the 

President's Committee To Appraise 

Employment and Unemployment

Statistics. 

AVERAGE HOURS AND EARNINGS.- 

Gross average hourly and weekly earnings, and average weekly hours, for production or nonsupervisory workers, are issued currently by the Bureau for about 352 industries on a national basis. Average weekly overtime hours are published currently for 146 manufacturing industry groups. Through the cooperative State program, similar data are made available for all States and the more important metropolitan areas. These statistics are reported monthly in Employment and Earnings 

and Monthly Report on the Labor Force.

OCCUPATIONAL STATISTICS AND ANAL- 

YSIS. Reports are published on the long-range employment outlook in important occupations and industries. 

Data on employment trends, earnings, hours, industrial hazards, collective bargaining agreements, and technological trends collected by the Bureau are included for guidance purposes, together with information from other Government and private sources. Conclusions of these studies are published in the Occupational Outlook Quar terly, a periodical issued four times in the school year, and biennially in the 

Occupational Outlook Handbook. 

Plans are now being implemented to obtain current employment statistics by occupation, with the goal of developing a regular annual statistical series on employment in about 100 of the most important professional, technical skilled, and clerical occupations. Such data are needed to refine estimates of future occupational requirements and opportunities, to evaluate the impac of automation and technological change and shift in demand on the occupational structure of the labor force, and to measure the effectiveness of training and education programs in meeting needs for skilled workers. 

WAGES AND INDUSTRIAL RELA- 

TIONS.-Occupational wage survey are made annually in 85 major labor areas. These studies provide infor mation on the level and distribution of wages and salaries for office clerical professional and technical, mainte nance and power plant, and custodial warehousing, and shipping occupa tional categories. Work schedules and supplementary wage benefits are also summarized in these studies. A more comprehensive national survey of salaries for professional, administrative technical, and clerical occupations is made annually.

Occupational wage surveys are made in selected industries covering majo manufacturing and nonmanufacturing

industries over a 5-year cycle. A few industries are studied annually; most industries, however, are studied at 3to 5-year intervals. Information is provided on a national and regional basis and for selected areas of concentration. Work schedules and supplementary wage benefits are also summarized in these studies. Annual surveys are made in 68 cities of wage rates agreed upon in union contracts for a limited number of occupations in printing and publishing, local streetcar and bus operations, the building trades, and motor trucking. Quarterly data are available for 100 cities for seven selected occupations in the construction trades.

Distributions of production and related workers and of other nonsupervisory employees by straight-time average hourly earnings are periodically established in studies that provide national and regional estimates for manufacturing and selected nonmanufacturing industries for minimum wage legislation and other purposes. 

Information on current trends in wage rates and wage practices is presented in a monthly report summarizing current wage settlements. In addition, statistical summaries are prepared quarterly and annually. Chronologies showing the historical development of wage rate changes are presented for important bargaining situations in selected industries. A series of indexes of changes in wages and salaries for selected occupational groups are maintained. 

Studies of employer expenditures on selected fringe benefits and of the composition of payroll hours are made over a 3-year cycle in manufacturing and in selected nonmanufacturing industries.

The Bureau publishes analyses of union agreements in individual industries and agreement provisions concerning such subjects as arbitration and grievances, job security issues, and wage provisions. Similar studies of health, insurance, and pension plans, and other employee benefit plans and of the substantive provisions of union constitutions are also made. Current statistics on work stoppages resulting from industrial disputes are issued monthly with detailed analyses available annually. The Bureau publishes a biennial Directory of National and International Labor Unions in the United States, and studies of union membership, structure, and procedures. The Bureau maintains a file of current union contracts and constitutions which is used as factual background material by unions, employers, and conciliation agencies in the settlement of industrial disputes, and as a guide to the preparation of new agreements. 

PRODUCTIVITY MEASUREMENT.-The 

Bureau publishes annual indexes of output per man-hour and unit manhour requirements for the private economy and broad economic sectors such as agriculture, manufacturing, and nonmanufacturing. Annual indexes are published comparing trends in productivity with those of employment costs per hour, employment costs per unit of output, and prices for the total private nonagricultural and manufacturing sectors of the economy. Indexes are also prepared for selected industries in manufacturing and nonmanufacturing relating output to the manhours of production workers and of all employees.

STUDIES IN TECHNOLOGY.-The 

Bureau conducts studies of technological developments and automation and their implications for productivity and manpower requirements. These studies explore the technological outlook among industries and the impact of major innovations across industry lines. 

These studies also deal with the adjustments made by plants introducing new kinds of equipment, including planning, training, and transfer of workers, the outlook for innovations and for technological developments in different industries, with the projected impact on productivity and changes in

LABOR REQUIREMENTS.-Studies of the importance of construction in generating employment include estimates for direct, on-site construction activities and for indirect, off-site activities such as manufacturing, mining, and transportation. They also provide information on the kind of construction labor used, the timing of construction, and the kinds of materials used. 

INDUSTRIAL HAZARDS.-The Bureau conducts quarterly surveys on work injuries in manufacturing, and annual surveys in both manufacturing and nonmanufacturing in a large number of industries. National estimates are prepared annually for all disabling work injuries, by extent of disability for major industry groups. Special studies are made in industries with high accident rates, to determine accident causes and thereby to stimulate accident prevention programs in the industries studied. 

Technical services are extended to State agencies to assist them in the development of better accident statistics. Currently, State-Federal cooperative injury rate surveys are conducted in 13 States.

PRICES AND LIVING CONDITIONS.- 

The Bureau is the principal agency of the Federal Government concerned with price statistics outside the field of agriculture. It is also responsible for conducting surveys of family expenditures and incomes, developing family budget studies, and analyzing changes in levels and standards of living. 

The Bureau computes a Consumer Price Index for the Nation which is published monthly. Retail prices are collected regularly in 56 cities for food and for other items such as clothing, house furnishings, miscellaneous goods and services, and rents. In addition to a U.S. index, city indexes are published monthly for the 5 largest cities and quarterly for 18 other cities.

The Wholesale Price Index includes 

Region primary market prices of over 2,200 raw materials, semimanufactured goods, and manufactured goods, divided into 15 major groups, 85 subgroups, 288 product classes. These data are also classified into 34 indexes by stage of processing, 8 indexes by durability of product, and 27 other special purpose indexes. The Bureau maintains records of price quotations for over 7,000 series for goods sold in primary markets. Primary market price indexes are published weekly and monthly. In addition, it publishes a daily index of spot market prices. 

Studies of consumer expenditures and income are conducted from time to time. Such studies were made in 66 cities during 1961 and 1962, and in 5 cities in the spring of 1964. Standard budgets are developed at irregular intervals, the last being for 1959.

The Solicitor of Labor The Solicitor has responsibility for all the legal activities of the Department, for the coordination and preparation of the Department's legislative proposals, reports and testimony on proposed legislation, including executive branch clearances, and for the administration of the Davis-Bacon and related acts except as specifically reserved to the Secretary. He serves as legal adviser to the Secretary and other officials of the Department. statistics in general and unit labor costs and labor force statistics, in particular are also studied and reported on. 

In cooperation with the Bureau of 

International Labor Affairs, the Bureau of Labor Statistics provides opportunities for labor statisticians from other countries to study its methods and on request sends consultants to countries undertaking new statistical programs in the labor field. 

Office of the Solicitor The Solicitor is the chief law officer of the Department of Labor. With the assistance of the Deputy Solicitor, he directs and supervises the legal work of the entire Department. Responsible to him is an immediate staff of assistants and attorneys in Washington and in the field offices of the Department throughout the United States and Puerto Rico.

The Solicitor is also empowered to perform the duties of the Secretary of Labor in certain instances. Pursuant to delegation of authority from the Secretary, he exercises final authority in the 

Department over the withdrawal of originals and copies of files, records, and documents of the Department, in determining the necessity of publishing documents in the Federal Register, and over tort claims arising out of the Department's activities; performs administrative and interpretative functions under the Davis-Bacon Act and related prevailing-wage statutes, the 

Copeland Act, the Contract Work 

Hours Standards Act, and the functions of the Department under Reorganization Plan 14 of 1950, except those functions that have been delegated to the Wage Appeals Board. 

Among the major Department activities serviced by the Solicitor are those relating to manpower development and training and work training programs for youth under the poverty program, minimum wages and maximum hours, equal pay, child labor, employment security, adjustment assistance for workers, registration of farm labor contractors, veterans readjustment assistance program, workmen's compensation, veterans' reemployment rights, apprenticeship training, safety and health on Government contracts and of longshoremen, labormanagement laws, welfare and pension plans reporting and disclosure, and international labor affairs, and all equal opportunity obligations.

The Solicitor's Office interprets statutes administered or coordinated in the Department, drafts rules and regulations implementing such statutes, and furnishes legal services in connection with hearings and other administrative proceedings leading to formulation of rules and regulations implementing such statutes. The Solicitor is in charge of the litigation of the Department. He represents the Secretary of Labor in the

* b) ill!! institution and prosecution of all civil court actions involving the Fair Labor Standards Act, including preparation of briefs and argument of appellate cases and interpreting, instituting, and conducting proceedings involving the Equal Pay Act. His Office assists in the preparation, trial, and briefing of criminal cases under the Fair Labor Standards Act, and civil actions to recover damages under the Public Contracts Act, the McNamara-O'Hara 

Service Contract Act, the Mexican labor program, and the Immigration Act; represents the Department officials in administrative hearings; and performs legal services in the preparation, institution and trial of enforcement cases in the Federal courts under the Labor-Management Reporting and 

Disclosure Act and Welfare and Pension Plans Disclosure Act; assists in litigation arising under the Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' Compen sation Act and the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Executive Order 11246; and represents the Bureau of Em ployees' Compensation before the Employees' Compensation Appeals Board

Assistant Secretary for Administration 

The Assistant Secretary for Adminstration has responsibility for the Department's budgetary and fiscal management, personnel management, administrative management, organization, the Library, and administrative services activities. He is assisted by the , who serves as the Department's Budget 

Officer and Comptroller, and the Assistant Assistant Secretary who serves as Director of Personnel. 

Office of the Assistant Secretary for

Administration The Office directs and coordinates all matters of administration and management in the Department and handles or supervises all contacts with 

Congress on budget matters. 

It reviews, evaluates, and approves proposed and existing programs to assure compliance with Department policies, plans, and budgetary directives; determines amounts and adequacy of presentation of budget estimates and apportionments. The 

Office develops, reviews, and approves organization structures within the several bureaus, is responsible for the management and coordination of planning-programing-budgeting activities, and promulgates departmental regulations and procedures governing all budget, fiscal management, management analysis, and office service functions. It develops and maintains all major relationships outside the Department on administration and management matters and coordinates contacts with the Bureau of the 

Budget, except those involving substantive legislation.

Services concerned with real property, space, communications, messenother laws under the field jurisdiction of the Department. ger service, central mail room facilities, parking space facilities, travel arrangements, local transportation facilities, procurement of articles and services, centralized duplicating and printing, and centralized stock and shipping rooms are provided by the Office on a departmentwide basis. Preparation of the budget for the Office of the Secretary and certain bureaus and offices and the provision of centralized accounting and payroll services are also responsibilities of the Office. 

Responsibility for the development and coordination of all plans and procedures necessary to provide management, fiscal, and administrative services for the execution of the mobilization and civil defense responsibility of the Department, including communications, establishing and maintaining relocation sites, safeguarding records and providing physical security measures, rests with the Office.

The Office directs and coordinates the personnel program of the Department and is responsible for the standards, procedures, and methods under which the program operates. It also directs management programs to improve employee-management relations, employee morale, employee training and utilization, and employee work performance appraisal and improvement.

LIBRARY.-The Library is a special ized collection of over 400,000 books, periodicals, and pamphlets on labor and related subjects. It provides reference service to the staff of the Department and to the public, circulates books and periodicals to the staff, and lends material to other libraries.

KUISUALS WHI HUU!**  Department of Health, Education, and 

Welfare was created by Reorganization 

Plan 1 of 1953. Under provisions of the act approved April 1, 1953 (67 

Stat. 18; 5 U. S. C. 623), the Plan became effective on April 11, 1953. The 

Plan abolished the Federal Security 

Agency, created by Reorganization Plan I of 1939, and transferred all functions of the Federal Security Ad ministrator to the Secretary of Health,

Education, and Welfare and all components of the Agency to the Department.

SECRETARY.-The Secretary of 

Health, Education, and Welfare, as the head of an executive department, reports directly to the President, supervises and directs the Department, and carries out Federal responsibilities in relation to three federally aided cor porations: American Printing House for the Blind, Gallaudet College, and 

Howard University.

UNDER 

SECRETARY.-The Under

In the administration of Department Planning, Programming, and Budgeting System by: developing long-range objectives, evaluating alternative means of achieving the objectives, conducting cost benefit studies, providing staff leadership in the conduct of economic and systems analyses on a Department-wide basis. 

GENERAL COUNSEL. The General 

Counsel provides legal advice and Opinions; coordinates the preparation and clearance of reports on pending and proposed legislation; and provides advice and assistance in the drafting of proposed regulations.

Field activities of 

Public Health Service 

Regulations, Title 42, Chapter I]  

Public Health Service has its origin in an act of July 16, 1798 (ch. 77, 1 Stat. 

605), authorizing marine hospitals for the care of American merchant seamen. Subsequent legislation has vastly broadened the scope of its activities. 

The Public Health Service Act of July 1, 1944 (58 Stat. 682; 42 U. S. C. 

201), consolidated and revised substantially all existing legislation relating to the Public Health Service, including title VI of the Social Secu rity Act, and provided for greater assistance to States, for coordinated research, for establishment of a national tuberculosis control program, and for expansion of the commissioned corps. The basic Public Health Serv ice legal responsibilities have been broadened and expanded many times since 1944. 

Among the more important functions added have been those for the the Department which do not operate out of a regional office are subject toreview by the regional director particularly with reference to public and intergovernmental relations. The De partment maintains nine regional offices. control and prevention of air pollution; expanded fellowship and training programs; loans to students in the health professions; grants to States for planning comprehensive mental retardation programs; and the administration of construction grants for hospitals and medical facilities, health research facilities, teaching facilities for health personnel, research centers and other facilities for the mentally retarded, and mental health centers. 

PURPOSE.-The Public Health Serv ice, under the direction of the Surgeon General, is the Federal agency specifically charged with responsibilities for protecting and improving the health of the people of the Nation. It is also responsible for collaborating with gov ernments of other countries and with international organizations in world health activities. The major functions of the Service are: (1) to conduct and support research and training in the medical and related sciences, and in public health methods and administra tion; (2) to provide medical and hospital services to persons authorized to receive care from the Service, to aid in the development of the Nation's hospi tal and related facilities, and to prevent the introduction of communicable diseases into the United States and its possessions; and (3) to assist the 

States and other governments in the application of new knowledge for the prevention and control of disease the maintenance of a healthful envi ronment, and the development of com munity health services. 

ORGANIZATION.-The activities of the Service are organized into four bureaus: Office of the Surgeon Gen eral, Bureau of Medical Services, Bureau of State Services, and National Institutes of Health; and the National 

Library of Medicine. 

The National Advisory Health 

Council and the advisory councils established for each major program area provide overall advice and policy guidance to the Surgeon General and review all research grant applications in their area of competence. Advice

and consultation is also secured from other advisory groups, from the Board of Regents of the National Library of 

Medicine, and from the Conference of 

State and Territorial Health Officers. 

In order to maintain direct contact with State and local authorities, with Held offices of other Federal agencies, and with other official and nonofficial organizations concerned with its activiies, the Service maintains a staff in the regional offices of the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare. 

These staffs are headed by regional health directors who represent the Surgeon General in interpreting and carying out the broad policies of the 

Service. The regional health director is assisted by two associate regional health directors, one representing the programs of community health and the other, the programs of environmental health. The regional staffs work with 

State authorities in developing and maintaining plans, programs, and budgets for Federal-State cooperative health programs.

Office of the Surgeon General The Office of the Surgeon General s a bureau composed mainly of staff ervices for the three operating bureaus and for the Surgeon General in his Overall management of the organization. Its various divisions and offices assist in (1) studying the health needs of the Nation and coordinating Service programs; (2) coordinating grant policies of the Service; (3) promoting che communication of scientific infornation; (4) providing overall program and policy direction to Service activities in the international health field and in the planning, negotiation, and administration of Service responsibilities for international health services with Federal agencies and international organizations; (5) directing and coordinating the Service's information, publications, and public inquiries programs; (6) developing general plans and programs under which personnel administration will be carried on within -24 the Service; (7) managing budget and fiscal activities; (8) carrying out a comprehensive internal audit program; (9) providing for the management of all areas of general services; (10) facilitating organizational and procedural improvements and the general management of the Service; (11) supervising 

Public Health Service regional organizations and coordinating Public Health 

Service Federal-State activities; (12) preparing the Nation to meet the health and water needs of the civilian population in the event of a national disaster; and (13) assuming that health facilities and programs which receive Federal support are conducted on a nondiscriminatory basis. 798-477-66- 

THE NATIONAL CENTER FOR HEALTH STATISTICS.-The Center serves as the principal statistical arm of the Public Health Service and one of the major general purpose statistical organizations of the Government. This organization conducts continuing surveys and special studies of the Nation's population to determine the extent of illness and disability and to gather information related to these conditions.

Areas of interest include the amounts and type of medical services received, the economic and social impact of illness and disability and methods of financing family health care. Such information establishes a current picture of the Nation's health and serves as a basis for predicting health trends.

The Center is also the principal instrument of Federal Government cooperation with the States in the collection of vital statistics (births, deaths, marriages, and divorces) and is the only source of national tabulation and analysis of such data. The Center also sponsors cooperative studies in foreign countries which provide useful comparative statistical data.

The Bureau of Medical Services is the medical arm of the Public Health

Medical care is provided eligible beneficiaries through a system of Public Health Service hospitals, outpatient clinics, and offices located throughout the United States where seamen employed on vessels of U.S. Registry, Coast Guard and other uniformed services personnel, and other legal beneficiaries receive hospitalization, medical and dental care, and preventive health services. In addition, dependents of uniformed services personnel are entitled to medical care and emergency dental care at such hospitals and outpatient clinics. Public laws and regulations to prevent the introduction of quarantinable and other dangerous communicable diseases into the United States are implemented through a system of worldwide epidemiological vigilance and inspection of arriving persons, animals, and things at ports and airports involved in international traffic. The medical provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act to exclude persons who present a danger to public health or a probability of an economic burden to public funds are implemented by medical examinations of aliens performed abroad, and by medical inspec tions at ports of arrival. Bureau of State Services 

The Bureau of State Services is the principal operating bureau of the Serv ice for Federal-State and interstate health programs. It gives general direc tion to activities in the two broad areas of Community Health and Environ mental Health designed to aid the States and communities in developing, establishing, and maintaining effective programs for the prevention, treatment, and control of diseases and for

the prevention or control of environmental health hazards.

Within these areas, the Bureau conducts research; provides training; furnishes consultation and technical assistance to States and localities; conducts field surveys, investigations, and demonstrations; provides emergency disaster and epidemic aid to States; enforces corrective measures under certain statutes; conducts public information and education programs; and administers various grant and student loan programs. 

COMMUNITY HEALTH.-Bureau pro grams in this area are concerned with: (1) development of techniques for application of scientific observations in fields of biology and medicine; (2) social, economic, and behavioral aspects of major health problems; (3) services, including the professional the professional health aspects of the Health Insurance for the Aged Program and the Federal- 

State Medical Assistance Program, strengthening of home health care services provided by public and private agencies, and health services for domesic migratory agricultural workers and their families; (4) development and effective utilization of professional, technical, and auxiliary health manpower; (5) training of professional health personnel, including loans and scholarships for students in medical, dental, nursing, osteopathic, pharmaceutical, and related health professional schools and grants for improving the quality of health professions schools; (6) planning and construction of hospitals and related medical facilities, including facilities for the mentally retarded, appropriate to needs of communities; and (7) construction of teaching facilities for students in medicine, dentistry, nursing, public health, optometry, podiatry, and pharmacy. These programs include control of chronic diseases such as heart disease, cancer, diabetes, and arthritis and the dissemination of information on the hazards of smoking; control of communicable diseases, including tuberculosis and venereal diseases; eradication of certain disease vectors; services to domestic and foreign public health laboratories; prevention and control of injuries including the dissemination of information concerning the accidental ingestion of poisonous substances; conservation of sight, hearing, and speech and control of mental retardation and other neurological disorders; development and coordination of community health programs to remedy and alleviate problems of the chronically ill and aged; provision of consultation on nursing home and noninstitutional care services; administration of health programs in the fields of dental and nursing services and resources; support and conduct of research, experiments, and demonstrations relating to the development, utilization, and coordination of services, facilities, and resources of hospitals, and other medical facilities; and continuing education for the health professions including the operation of the PHS Medical Audiovisual Facility. 

ENVIRONMENTAL HEALTH.-Bureau programs in this area are concerned with: (1) the conduct and support of research to determine the nature, methods for effective measurement, and the health effects of environmental contaminants, including the total or cumulative effect as well as the individual effects on man; (2) the development of techniques and methods for practical control programs and for the maintenance of a healthful environment; (3) the study of political, social, and economic factors related to urbanization and metropolitan complexes as they affect environmental health, in order to develop effective methods of organization and administration in this field; (4) the development and effective utilization of professional and technical manpower and other resources for the broad field of environmental health; and (5) the administration of interstate quarantine regulations, and air pollution abatement measures. Federal Security Administrator. Other duties have subsequently been delegated to or transferred from the Administration by law or Presidential order. On July 26, 1965, the Social Security Administration was reorganized to accommodate the new health insurance programs.

PURPOSE. The Social Security Ad ministration administers the Federal old-age, survivors and disability insurance programs (title II of the Social Security Act, as amended, and title VII and XI of that act as they pertain

AIPUARONES KATI LIKIUI?!! 

to the Social Security Administration), health insurance for the aged programs 

(title XVIII of the Social Security 

Act), and the Federal credit union.

program (Federal Credit Union Act). 

It is responsible for studying problems of poverty, insecurity, and the health care needs of the aged and the contributions that can be made to their solution by social insurance and related programs and for making recommendations as to the most effective methods of improving social and economic security through social insurance. 

The purpose of retirement, survivors, and disability insurance programs is to provide continuing income for individuals and their families as partial replacement of earnings lost through old-age or disability retirement or death. These programs provide for the coverage of almost all persons engaged in gainful employment, including the military, the major exceptions being Federal civilian employees under a retirement system; and domestics, agricultural workers, and self-employed persons having very low earnings. Entitlement to benefits is determined from the insured status of the individual; the age and relationship of the individual and his dependents; the application for such benefits; and in the case of disability benefits, the extent and expected duration of disability. Benefits are payable monthly in amounts related to the average monthly earnings of the insured person. A lump sum death benefit is payable under certain conditions. 

The health insurance program (hospital and supplementary medical insurance) provides the aged with basic protection against the costs of hospital care, and physicians' services, and certain other health and medical services. All social security and railroad retirement beneficiaries are entitled to hospital insurance benefits when they attain age 65. (For an interim period most persons who are age 

65, or will attain age 65 in the near future, but who are not eligible for social security or railroad retirement benefits are also entitled to protection under hospital insurance.) Persons who have attained age 65 are eligible to enroll for the supplementary medi cal insurance, sharing the premium payment with the Government. 

The Federal credit union program promotes thrift by encouraging cooperative, systematic saving and by mak ing credit available in the short-term, small loan field at reasonable rates of interest, for credit union members. To accomplish these purposes, Federal credit unions provide convenient facilities for encouraging the development of habits of consistent, regular saving out of current earnings.

The Office of the Commissioner includes the immediate staff of the Commissioner, Deputy Commissioner, and
