Secretary's reorganization of January 28, 1963, created the Welfare Administration and assigned to it the following components and their pro grams: the Bureau of Family Services, the Children's Bureau, the Office of 

Juvenile Delinquency and Youth De velopment, the Cuban Refugee Program Staff and the Office of Aging, together with administration of titles 

VII and XI of the Social Security Act as they apply to the Welfare Administration. The Office of Aging was abolished September 30, 1965, and its functions were assumed by the new Administration on Aging. regional representatives of the program bureaus (disability, Federal credi unions, health, hearings and appeals and retirement and survivors insur ance, plus the regional representative with direct line responsibility over district offices). The regional assistant commissioners who report to the Commissioner through the Assistant 

Commissioner, Field, coordinate and provide leadership to the activities of the regional representatives. 

PURPOSE.-The Welfare Adminis tration is responsible for administering the programs of the Federal Government pertaining to assistance to individuals and families in need, the provision of welfare and medical assistance and services for children, the aging, and other groups, and maternal and child health services. It is responsible for studying the causes, prevention, and reduction of dependency, matters pertaining to child life, the welfare and medical needs of children, the aging, and other groups, and for making studies and recommendations as to the most effective method of providing social and economic security through social welfare programs. 

The programs are primarily Federal- State in nature, with the States receiving Federal grants-in-aid in return for operating in accordance with Federa standards. In the welfare areas of research, demonstration projects, consul tation, stimulation, and coordination the relationships of the Welfare Administration extend to State, local, and voluntary agencies, community groups, and universities.

CENTRAL ORGANIZATION.-The Wel fare Administration includes the Office of the Commissioner, the Cuban Refugee Program Staff, the Office of Ju venile Delinquency and Youth Devel opment, the Bureau of Family Services, and the Children's Bureau. 

REGIONAL AND FIELD ORGANIZA- 

TION. A regional representative and appropriate supporting staff is assigned to each of the Department's nine regional offices for each of the following program areas: family services, child welfare, and maternal and child health. 

These regional staffs are established to provide consultation and services to State and local agencies and organiza. tions in their program areas, and, to the maximum extent consistent with effective management, to provide decentralized program administration. 

Office of the Commissioner 

The Office of the Commissioner directs and coordinates the Welfare Administration program and performs

basic research covering the broader phase of social welfare. This includes the formulation of policy, coordination of interprogram activities, review and coordination of administrative management activities, and certification of compliance with State laws, plans, and operations with Federal requirements, and approval of grants to States. 

The Office of the Commissioner provides training services for fellows and scholars from other countries, cooperates in overseas projects through recruitment of experts and continuing technical supervision, participates in research and other technical exchange with international organizations and with other countries, and assists in the preparation for international meetings on subject matter of concern to the 

Welfare Administration. 

The Office of the Commissioner also formulates broad research and statistical goals and policies, conducts the basic studies necessary to analyze aspects of social welfare that are beyond the immediate scope of the bureaus, and reviews and integrates the tatistical and analytic work of program bureaus. Its activities are concentrated on overall social, financial, and economic aspects, the relation of he programs to other social welfare and related measures, and the development of findings and recommendations on the most effective methods of providing social and economic security hrough social welfare programs. The 

Office of the Commissioner also pro- -ides a secretariat for making contracts with or grants to States and public and ther nonprofit organizations and agenies for paying part of the cost of reearch or demonstration projects in the eld of social welfare and related prorams. 

Cuban Refugee Program Staff 

The Cuban Refugee Program was stablished in accordance with the resident's letter to the Secretary dated anuary 27, 1961, and continues under the Migration and Refugee Assistance Act of 1962 (76 Stat. 121; 22 U.S.C. 

2601 note) and Executive Order 11077 of January 22, 1963. The Staff administers an emergency program which includes: (1) financial assistance to supply basic essentials (food, clothing, and shelter) to needy refugees; (2) financial assistance in relocating refugees from Miami, Fla., to homes and jobs elsewhere in the country; (3) emergency health services; (4) assistance to the public schools of Dade 

County (Miami, Fla.) in providing instruction to the refugee children as well as English instruction and vocational training to adults; (5) loans to refugee students in college and funds for English and refresher courses for doctors and other professional persons; and (6) care of minors unaccompanied by relatives. These programs are carried out through a Federal Cuban 

Refugee Emergency Center in Miami, four voluntary relocation agencies, and a variety of Federal, State, and local agencies and organizations. 

Office of Juvenile Delinquency and Youth Development 

This office was established to carry out the demonstration project and training grant program provided in the 

Juvenile Delinquency and Youth Of fenses Control Act of 1961 (75 Stat. 

572; 42 U.S.C. 2541 note). It operates a grant and contract program for the support of demonstration projects aimed at the prevention and control of juvenile delinquency and a program to train personnel who work, or who are preparing to work in the field of juvenile delinquency. Proposed studies and projects are reviewed and selected for support in terms of their potential in providing new and promising ways of dealing with the problem. Methods of overcoming current fragmented approaches to delinquency prevention and control are encouraged. Technical assistance is also provided to State, local, and private nonprofit agencies.

Bureau of Family Services 

[For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 45, Chapter II] The Bureau of Family Services administers grants to help States provide public assistance under the Social Security Act for old-age assistance and medical assistance for the aged (title I), aid to families with dependent children (title IV), aid to the blind (title X), and aid to the permanently and totally disabled (title XIV). States may also provide for the aged, blind and disabled and/or the medically needy aged under one program (title 

XVI). Effective January 1, 1966, a new program of grants to States for medical assistance programs (title 

XIX) was established.

The Bureau reviews and approves 

State plans for public assistance; reviews State estimates, and certifies to the United States Treasury Federal grants to the States;

reviews the oper- ation of State plans for continuing conformity with the Social Security Act; collects, analyzes, and publishes data on the operation of public assistance in the States, including general assistance, and provides technical help to States to improve their programs. 

Public assistance includes financial aid, medical care, and other social services to help recipients achieve their potentialities for self-care, self-support, and strong family life. The extent of financial aid and the provision of services vary between States, reflecting the State's traditions, legislative and administrative structures, community concern, and assistance appropriations. 

The State plan must provide for the program to be in effect in all parts of the State, and for State financial participation. A single State agency must administer the program or supervise its administration. The plan must provide for such methods of administration, including a merit system covering personnel, and for submitting such reports as the Department finds necessary for proper and efficient operation.

The plan must provide for keeping personal information confidential (except as modified by section 618 of the 

Revenue Act of 1951, 65 Stat. 569). 

It cannot set residence and citizenship requirements beyond those named in Federal law. It must provide for a hearing before the State agency for those who are not satisfied with the action on their cases. In determining need and the amount of the payment, the State must take into account any other income or resources of the person claiming aid. In aid to the blind, some of the blind person's earned income is disregarded, and in medical assistance for the aged, a reasonable amount of income and resources is permitted as determined by each State. 

The Social Security Act defines the scope of Federal participation, but does not limit the breadth of State operations. The State may claim Federal money to help needy people living in their own homes, in private institutions, and in public medical institutions. The State's payments to assistance recipients for maintenance must be in the form of money. Some medical costs are included in the money pay ment but most are paid by the agency directly to the medical-care suppliers. 

Under assignment, the Bureau is responsible for assisting the States in developing and maintaining plans for a state of readiness for welfare services in a civil defense emergency, and for continuity and restoration of peacetime welfare programs; performs welfare planning activities in regard to refugees and immigrants, and the repatriation of American nationals from abroad. 

The Economic Opportunity Act of 

1964 (title V) resulted in the Bureau being assigned responsibility for a work experience and training program to help unemployed persons-both those receiving or likely to receive public assistance.

Children's Bureau  Regulations, Title 

42, Chapter II] 

The Children's Bureau was created by the act approved April 9, 1912 (37 

Stat. 79, as amended; 42 U. S. C. 191 et seq.) (see also appendix A).

The purpose of the Bureau is to investigate and report on all matters related to child life and to increase opportunity for the full development of all children by promoting their health and social welfare. It administers title 

V of the Social Security Act. 

The Bureau cooperates with national, State, and local organizations and agencies, both public and voluntary, in planning for the development and extension of services for children and youth.

Division of Health Services, grants to 

State health agencies for extending and improving health services for mothers and children, authorized by title V, part 1, of the Social Security Act. 

These agencies use the funds to provide health promotion services such as maternity clinics where women get the advice of doctors, nurses, nutritionists, and medical social workers; visits of public health nurses to homes before and after babies are born; well child clinics for child health supervision where mothers can get competent advice on the health care of their babies and preschool children; pediatric clinics; school health programs that spot the youngsters who need medical or dental treatment and help them get it; dental care for children and pregnant women; and immunizations against preventable diseases. Most 

States conduct special clinics for mentally retarded children where diagnostic, evaluation, counseling, treatment, and followup services are provided. 

The Bureau provides medical, dental, nursing, nutrition, physical-therapy, In carrying out the responsibilities assigned by its organic act, the Bureau makes studies of conditions that are hazards to the well-being of children. and of the effectiveness of measures aimed at preventing and alleviating such conditions. On request, it gives advisory service to State and local agencies regarding research and methods of conducting programs aimed at promoting the health and welfare of children. The Bureau provides a clearinghouse of research in child life by collecting and distributing information regarding research studies under way in universities, schools, hospitals, child research centers, and other public and private agencies throughout the country.

The Bureau issues both technical and popular publications. Most widely known of its publications for parents s Infant Care. Its Statistical Series presents data on operations of child health and welfare programs and staistics on the conditions of child life. 

For a representative list of publicacions, see appendix B.

The Bureau administers, through its and medical-social consultation services to State health agencies administering such services.

Through its Division of Health Serv ices, the Bureau administers a 5-year program of grants to provide maternity and infant care, authorized by title V, part 4, of the Social Security Act. State health agencies or, with the consent of such agencies, the health agencies of any political subdivisions of the States use these grants to provide medical care to women who during the maternity period are unlikely to receive necessary health care because they are from families with low incomes or for other reasons. In addition to medical care for the mother, health care for mothers and infants following childbirth is included. The health care is available particularly to prospective mothers who have or are likely to have conditions associated with childbearing which increase the hazards to the

health of mothers or their infants, including those which may cause physical or mental defects in the infants. 

The Bureau also administers, through its Division of Health Services, grants to State crippled children's agencies for extending and improving services for crippled children, authorized by title V, part 2, of the Social Security Act. These agencies, usually in State health or welfare departments, use the funds to locate handicapped children, to provide diagnostic services, and then to see that each child gets the medical care, hospitalization, and continuing care that he needs by a variety of professional people. The 

Bureau provides consultation service to the State agencies on methods and procedures for the early casefinding, the diagnosis, and medical treatment of crippled children and on the development of programs for the care of children with special types of crippling conditions such as epilepsy, poliomyelitis, rheumatic fever, congenital heart disease, and cerebral palsy. 

The Bureau also administers, through its Division of Health Services, special project grants to provide comprehensive health care and services for children of school age, or for preschool children, particularly in areas with concentrations of low-income families. 

Projects provide screening, diagnosis, preventive services, treatment, correction of defects and aftercare for children in low-income families. These grants are available to the State health agency or, with its consent, to the health agency of any political subdivision of the State, to the State agency administering or supervising the crippled children's program, to schools of medicine (with appropriate participation by schools of dentistry) and to teaching hospitals affiliated with schools of medicine. 

In the fiscal year ending June 30, 1967, the Bureau will begin administering a program of grants to institutions of higher learning for training of professional personnel such as physicians, psychologists, nurses, dentists, and social workers for health and related care of crippled children, particularly mentally retarded children and those with multiple handicaps. The Bureau administers, through its Division of Social Services, grants to State public welfare agencies, authorized by title V, part 3, of the Social Security Act, to establish, extend, and strengthen child welfare services. In each State public welfare agency, the division responsible for services to children plans and directs the program for child welfare services. Federal funds are used mainly for State staff members to assist in the development of community child welfare programs, for child welfare workers in local communities to provide social services to children, for training of child welfare staffs, and for foster care for certain children who are the responsibility of public welfare agencies. In the administration of these grants the regional staff of the 

Division of Social Services participates in the development of State plans and gives advisory and consultant service to State public welfare agencies. 

Specialists develop guide materials and provide consultation to national, State, and local public and voluntary agencies in developing services to children in their own homes, foster family care, group care, and institutional care; adoption services; homemaker serv ices; day care services; services to unmarried mothers; and services to mentally retarded children as well. 

Specialists also advise on training of staff in child welfare programs and on State legislation relating to children. 

This division also administrates grants for training personnel for work in the field of child welfare by means of funds to institutions of higher learning for curriculum development, traineeships, and short-term training. The Bureau administers, through its Division of Research, child welfare research and demonstration grants for projects which are of regional or national significance and for demonstra-

on of new methods or facilities which ow promise of substantial contribuon to the advancement of child welre. The Division of Research also adinisters research grants for scientific udies that may contribute to the 

Ivancement of health services for others and children and improve the eration and effectiveness of maternal d child health and crippled chilen's services.

The Bureau offers technical assistace in the field of juvenile delinency to States and communities anning the extension, improvement, nd more effective coordination of the arious State and local services and cilities required for the location, eatment, and rehabilitation of delinent youth. Consultants are availole to advise on the training of ersonnel for these services; on the ontent, legislative bases, and admintration of juvenile delinquency prorams; and on such special types of rvices as police, juvenile courts, etention, diagnostic and reception enters, training schools, and group ork. PURPOSE. The Vocational Rehabil itation Administration is responsible for the administration of programs to increase the vocational rehabilitation of disabled persons and their greater utilization in gainful and suitable employment. The Administration cooperates with the States and private nonprofit organizations in providing these services to the handicapped. 

ACTIVITIES. This agency adminis ters a program of grants to States, which provides a wide range of services to disabled persons and a program licensing blind persons to operate vending stands on Federal or other property. It administers research and training programs to improve rehabilitation techniques and to increase the supply of professionally trained rehabilitation personnel. 

The States have broad authority and responsibility in carrying out their programs of vocational rehabilitation. The vocational rehabilitation program may be located under the board of education or vocational education in a separate agency concerned primarily with rehabilitation, or in a State agency which includes at least two other organizational units, each of which administers one or more of the major public education, public health, public welfare, or labor programs of the State. 

In each State which has a separate agency to serve the blind, this agency may function as the sole State agency responsible for administering that part of the State plan relating to rehabilitation of the blind.

The vocational rehabilitation program is in effect in the 50 States, the 

District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the 

Virgin Islands, and Guam. There are now 91 State agencies in all, 37 of which serve only the blind.

The disability insurance provisions of the Social Security Act authorize the payment of disability benefits to eligible disabled workers, their dependents, and to the disabled children (beyond age 18) of a retired, deceased, or disabled worker. State vocational rehabilitation agencies are responsible, under agreements with the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare, for preparing the determinations of disability for those individuals in the State who apply for social security disability benefits. All applicants for such benefits must also be referred to the State vocational rehabilitation agency for necessary vocational rehabilitation services to the end that the maximum number of such individuals may be rehabilitated into productive activity. Rehabilitation Act. The Vocational Rehabilitation Ad ministration is responsible for (1) a program of training for professional personnel and (2) research to advance knowledge of ways of overcoming handicapping conditions. For the training of professional personnel the Administration conducts a program of training grants to public and voluntary educational institutions and agencies and to individuals. Its objectives are (1) to enlarge the supply of trained personnel for the rehabilitation of physically or mentally handicapped persons; (2) to improve the knowledge and skills of personnel already engaged in rehabilitation services; and (3) to instill a better understanding of rehabilitation philosophy and process on the part of all students enrolled in basic professional training programs preparing personnel for work in rehabilitation services. Food and Drug Administration 

(200 C Street SW., Washington, D.C., 20024)  

Regulations, Title 21, Chapter I]  ame "Food and Drug Administraon" was first provided by the Agriultural Appropriation Act of 1931, pproved May 27, 1930 (46 Stat. 392), though similar law-enforcement inctions had been carried on under ifferent organizational titles since anuary 1, 1907, when the Food and rugs Act of 1906 (34 Stat. 768; 21 

J.S.C. 1-15) became effective. For a ore complete history of the Food and 

Drug Administration, see appendix A. 

PURPOSE. The Food and Drug dministration administers the Fedral Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act,

Tea Importation Act, Import Milk 

Act, Caustic Poison Act, Hazardous ubstances Labeling Act, and Filled Milk Act. Its activities are directed mainly toward promoting purity, tandard potency, and truthful and inormative labeling of consumer prodcts covered by this legislation. 

ORGANIZATION.-The Food and 

Drug Administration operates under he direction of the Commissioner of 'ood and Drugs, who is responsible to he Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare. Its Washington head quarters consist of executive, profesional, and service staffs located in the Office of the Commissioner and seven Bureaus which specialize in scientific esearch and analysis, medical evaluaion, and regulatory and voluntary compliance. To provide nationwide coverage, the United States is divided nto 18 district territories, each with headquarters manned by chemists and nspectors and fully equipped with Cesting laboratories. Within these district territories there are 58 inspection stations located in industrial concentrations. Additionally, five field stations span the United States, directing an expanded program for controlling illicit traffic in depressant and stimulant drugs. 

REGULATORY OPERATIONS.-Each field district is responsible for maintaining surveillance taining surveillance over practices regulated by the six basic laws. Factories are inspected for sanitary conditions, raw materials used, and controls exercised in compounding, processing, packaging, and labeling products destined for interstate shipment. When violations are suspected, shipments are reported for destination sampling as a basis for regulatory action. Each district also keeps under surveillance imports offered for entry at its ports, which are refused admission into the 

United States if they do not comply with applicable laws. Retail drugstores are kept under surveillance to prevent the dispensing of dangerous drugs without prescription. Field stations audit inventory records of manufacturers and distributors of depressant and stimulant drugs to prevent diversion of such drugs from legitimate distribution channels, conduct investigations to prevent illegal traffic of such drugs, and take appropriate regulatory action when violations of the Drug

Abuse Control Amendments are en countered.

The regulatory program is developed on a selective project basis, with primary attention accorded to violations most serious to the public welfare, and, so far as practicable, with simultaneous and uniform nationwide action. When domestic violations are found, the facts are reported to the Department of Justice with a recommendation for seizure, criminal prosecution, or injunction actions in the 

Federal courts.

EDUCATION AND VOLUNTARY COM- PLIANCE.-Mass media and individual communications, oral and written, are MEMBE Trucții

used to promote better understanding and cooperation by consumers and industry. This includes assistance to manufacturers who request it, through comments on labeling, and suggestions concerning changes in manufacturing procedures, improvements in sanitary controls, and other methods to bring about compliance with legal requirements. Consumers are advised of the intent of the FDA programs, what they should expect of FDA, and how they can protect themselves.

SCIENTIFIC INVESTIGATIONS.-The 

Washington laboratories (in addition to testing samples that requires specialized techniques and laboratory facilities not available at field laboratories) conduct fundamental research to determine characteristics of consumer products and production techniques, establish standards and tolerances for consumer protection, and develop methods capable of demonstrating violations in court actions. 

These investigations encompass the evaluation of the safety and efficacy of medicines; the toxicity of ingredients used in the manufacture of foods, drugs, and cosmetics; the safety of pesticidal and radioactive residues on food crops; the normal composition of all products covered by the acts administered; the potency of drugs and vitamins; and methods of processing, packaging, preserving, and storing products under adequate controls.

CONTROL OF NEW OR INVESTIGA- TIONAL DRUGS.-Applications for dis tributing new drugs (accompanied by the manufacturers' evidence establishing safety and effectiveness for use and adequacy of manufacturing controls) are evaluated and must be approved before each new drug is placed upo the market. New drugs are controlled during their investigational stage and after marketing is approved.

FOOD STANDARDS.-Intensive studies are made of composition, trade prac tices, and consumer understanding as a basis for formulating definitions and standards for foods that will promote honesty and fair dealing in the interest of the consumer.

Aging provides a strong central focus For the Federal Government's concern For the needs and problems of the aging population, and national leadership in meeting these needs and solving these problems.

OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATION.-The 

Office conducts the administrative, financial, and personnel management activities of the Administration; manages the financial aspects of grants and contracts administration; performs management appraisal of program operations; and provides advice to State agencies and project grantees on management problems.

OFFICE OF PROGRAM POLICY AND IN- FORMATION.-The Office analyzes and evaluates the impact of existing programs of the Administration on Aging and other agencies on the problems | MA

TAMING 

and needs of the aging; identifies needed improvements in program coordination, program content or coverage, or changes in program goals; develops proposals for such improvements in Administration programs; suggests improvements to other other agencies whose programs affect the aging; and develops liaison with these agencies to stimulate program coordination and mutual support. It provides secretariat services for the Advisory Committee on Older Americans and the President's Council on Aging. 

It also serves as a clearinghouse for information related to problems of the aged and aging, and information as to services and opportunities available; identifies gaps in coverage of these areas and takes action to meet the need or stimulate other sources to meet the need; prepares and publishes periodicals on aging programs and services; and prepares and disseminates educational materials directed primarily at professional aging specialists or the aging population.

OFFICE OF STATE AND COMMUNITY SERVICES.-This Office plans and carries out a program of Federal grants to States for community planning and coordination of programs for the aging, establishment of new or expansion of existing programs such as multipurpose senior centers, demonstrations, and training under title III of the Older Americans Act; develops policies, standards, and guides; provides consultation and technical assistance to the States and their political subdivisions on development of priorities, program development, and operation; reviews and approves State plans; evaluates the administration of State plans and advises on improvements; and stimulates State and local program innovation and progress in the extension of services and opportunities for the aging and the intermeshing of programs. It also plans and carries out for the Office of Economic Opportunity the stimulation, development, and supervision of locally initiated demonstration projects for the employmen of the elderly poor; develops models o desirable projects (e.g., Foster Grand parent Program); provides consulta tion on project development; evaluate project proposals and recommend funding by OEO; evaluates projec progress and recommends program and budget changes; evaluates projec results in terms of the desirability o continued support and use of finding in the development of model projects recommends on continuation of proj ects to OEO.

PURPOSE. Gallaudet College was established to provide a liberal higher education for deaf persons who need special facilities to compensate for their loss of hearing. The primary purpose of the college is to afford its students the intellectual and spiritual development that can be acquired through a study of the liberal arts and sciences. The college intends to produce men and women who have the power of sound independent judgment, and who are well informed about the world around them, about their civilization and its achievements, and about themselves as

Title 44, Chapter VII] (79 Stat. 667; 5 U.S.C. 642). The act, which became effective November 9, 1965, transferred to and vested in the 

Secretary of Housing and Urban De velopment all of the functions, powers, 387

and duties of the Housing and Home Finance Agency (including the Com munity Facilities Administration and the Urban Renewal Administration), of the Federal Housing Administration and the Public Housing Administra tion, and of the heads and other officers and offices of those agencies. PURPOSE. The Declaration of Pur pose of the Department of Housing and 

Urban Development Act declares that 

"the general welfare and security of the Nation and the health and living standards of our people require, as a matter of national purpose, sound development of the Nation's communities and metropolitan areas in which the vast majority of its people live and work. "To carry out such purpose, and in recognition of the increasing importance of housing and urban development in our national life, the Congress finds that establishment of an executive department is desirable to achieve the best administration of the principal programs of the Federal Government which provide assistance for housing and for the development of the Nation's communities; to assist the 

The Department is administered under the supervision and direction of the Secretary. The Secretary advises the President with respect to Federal programs and activities relating to housing and urban development; develops and recommends to the President policies for fostering the orderly 

President in achieving maximum coordination of the various Federal activities which have a major effect upon urban community, suburban, on metropolitan development; to encour age the solution of problems of hous ing, urban development, and mass transportation through State, county, town, village, or other local and private action, including promotion of interstate, regional, and metropolitan cooperation; to encourage the maximum contributions that may be made by vigorous private homebuilding and mortgage lending industries to housing urban development, and the nationa economy; and to provide for full and appropriate consideration, at the na tional level, of the needs and interests of the Nation's communities and of the people who live and work in them."

Regulations, Title 36, Chapter IV]  American Battle Monuments Com mission was created by act of Congress approved March 4, 1923 (42 Stat. 

1509; 36 U. S. C. 121). It derives its authority from this and subsequent acts and Executive orders (36 U. S. C. 

ch. 8; Executive Orders 6614 of February 26, 1934, 6690 of April 25, 1934, 9704 of March 14, 1946, and 10057 of 

May 14, 1949; and act approved June 

26, 1946, as amended, 60 Stat. 317, 70 Stat. 642; 36 U. S. C. 121). 

PURPOSE. The principal functions of the American Battle Monuments 

Commission are (1) to design and construct such American military cemeteries located outside the United States and its possessions as the Commission and the Secretary of the Army shall determine to be permanent cemeteries, to administer and maintain such cemeteries after they have been transferred to the Commission, and to erect and maintain works of architecture and art in them; (2) to prepare plans and estimates for the erection of suitable memorials to mark and commemorate the services of the American armed forces, and to erect and maintain memorials in the United States and at such places outside the United States where the American armed forces have served since April 6, 1917, or shall hereafter serve, as the Commission shall determine; (3) to maintain rosters of the burials and the recorded missing at the respective cemeteries; (4) to control as to materials and design, provide regulations for, and supervise the erection of, all memorial monuments and buildings in American cemeteries located outside of the United States and its possessions; and (5) to control as to materials and design, provide regulations for, and supervise the erection of, all memorial monuments and buildings commemorating the services of the American armed forces erected in any foreign country or political division thereof which may authorize the Commission to perform such functions. Approved.

JACOB L. DEVERS, Chairman.

States' Regional Representative Commission Executive Director General Counsel Technical Assistance Director Planning Director Program Director Special Assistant, Congressional Relations Public Information Director CREATION AND PURPOSE.-The Com mission was established by the Appala chian Regional Development Act of 1965 (79 Stat. 5; 40 U.S.C. App. 1) 

to develop plans for and coordinate the comprehensive programs for regional economic development authorized by the act. 

ORGANIZATION.-The 

Commission consists of the Governors or their representatives from each of the 12 Appalachian States, and a Federal Cochairman appointed by the President by and with the advice and consent of the Senate. The State members of the Commission elect a Cochairman from among their number. At the first Commission meeting, held April 19, 1965, the Appalachian Governors agreed to rotate the position of Cochairman every 6 months beginning July 1, 1965.

An Office of States' Regional Repre sentative on the Commission, created by the Governors, is headed by the 

States' Regional Representative who works full time in serving the interests of the Appalachian States on Commission matters. Functionally, this position is equivalent to the Federal Cochairman. The cost of maintaining this office is borne by the Appalachian 

States. 

The Commission staff structure, headed by the Executive Director who was appointed by the Commission, in cludes the General Counsel, a Program Division, a Planning Division, a Technical Assistance Division, a Public In- JOHN L. SWEENEY.

Because of the State-Federal nature of the Commission, its staff members are not Federal employees. After the second full Federal fiscal year following enactment of the Appalachian Act, the Commission expenses will be shared equally by the Federal Government and the Appalachian States; until then the Commission expenses will be assumed by the Federal 

Government. 

The act provides that all recommendations of the Commission must be approved by a majority of the Gover nors and by the Federal Cochairman.

Under the law, project proposals must originate in the States and be presented to the Commission; no project can be approved unless it is approved by the State concerned. The 

Commission staff processes the applications received from the States for projects under the various sections of the law.

ACTIVITIES.-The act authorizes a broad spectrum of economic development programs which will contribute to the growth of the region. [For regulations codified under Atomic Energy Commission, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 10, Chapter I; Title 41, Chapter 9]  

Atomic Energy Commission was estab lished by the Atomic Energy Act of 

1946 (60 Stat.

755), as amended by the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, as amended (68 Stat. 919; 42 U. S. C. 

2011 et seq.).

PURPOSE. The purpose of the 

Atomic Energy Act is to provide by national policy that the development, use, and control of atomic energy shall be directed to make the maximum contribution to the general welfare and to the common defense and security, and to promote world peace, increase the standard of living, and strengthen free competition in private enterprise. The 

Atomic Energy Commission has been established to provide and administer programs and to encourage private participation in such programs for research and development, international cooperation, production of atomic energy and special nuclear materials, and the dissemination of scientific and technical information. The Commission has responsibility to protect the health and safety of the public, and to regulate the control and use of source, byproduct, and special nuclear materials.

ORGANIZATION 

AND 

ACTIVITIES.- 

The Commission is composed of five members appointed by the President by and with the advice and consent of the Senate. One of the members is designated by the President as the 

Chairman. 

In the organization structure below the Commission, the licensing and regulatory functions of the AEC are separate and apart from the research, manufacturing, and promotional func tions. The Director of Regulation is responsible for the licensing and regu latory functions; the General Man ager, for the research, manufacturing, and promotional functions as well as the providing of staff services for the entire Commission structure. The quasi-judicial functions involved in regulation are not subject to direction by either the General Manager or the Director of Regulation but are reserved in the Commission assisted by atomic safety and licensing boards and by an Office of Hearing Examiners. 

The Board of Contract Appeals acts with finality for the Commission for the purpose of considering and deciding appeals from decisions or findings of fact of contracting officers.

The General Manager is the chief executive officer of the Commission who discharges such administrative and executive functions other than those involved in licensing and regulatory matters as the Commission may direct. The principal assistant to the 

General Manager is the Deputy General Manager who acts for the General Manager. The General Manager is assisted also by the Assistant General 

Manager, an Executive Assistant, an

Assistant to the General Manager, an 

Assistant to the General Manager for 

Program Analysis, and the Assistant

General Managers for International Activities, Research and Development, Reactors, Operations, Administration, and Plans and Production; the Director, Division of Military Application; and certain other staff divisions and offices which report directly to him on their own special functional areas. The 

Director of Regulation administers and coordinates the licensing and regula tory functions of the Commission. The 

Divisions of Compliance, State and Licensee Relations, Safety Standards, Materials Licensing, and Reactor Li censing report directly to him on their own special functional areas. 

Certain administrative and executive functions are assigned to various offices and divisions of the Headquarters. Managers in the various field offices have been delegated a substantial amount of authority to enter into con-

ATOMIC ENERGY COMMISSION 

403 tracts on behalf of the Commission, to act as representatives of the Commission for the administration of contracts executed under their authority or assigned to their offices, and to perform other special functions.

The General Advisory Committee, composed of nine members appointed from civilian life by the President, advises the Commission on scientific and technical matters relating to materials, production, and research and development.

The Military Liaison Committee consists of a chairman, appointed by the President by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, and of representatives from each of the Departments of Army, Navy, and Air Force in equal numbers. The Commission advises and consults with the Department of Defense, through the Committee, on matters relating to military applications of atomic weapons or atomic energy. 

The Advisory Committee on Reac tor Safeguards, consisting of a maximum of fifteen members appointed by the Commission, advises the Commission with regard to the hazards of proposed or existing reactor facilities and the adequacy of proposed reactor safety standards. Atomic safety and licensing boards are established by the Commission from time to time for the purpose of conducting such hearings as the Commission may direct and for making such decisions as it may authorize in proceedings for granting, suspending, revoking, or amending licenses or authorizations.

The nonregulatory operations of the Commission are carried out largely by industrial concerns and by private and public institutions under contract with the Commission, in accordance with the requirements and policies established by the Commission pursuant to the Atomic Energy Act. The principal production and research and development activities are conducted by contractors in facilities owned by the Commission.

Advisory committees to the Commission have been established in a variety of technical and other fields and most of them function on a continuing basis. 

Members include persons from business, industry, public, and educational institutions, and AEC and AEC contractors.

Major production facilities owned by the Commission are located at Oak 

Ridge, Tenn.; Richland, Wash.; and at sites near Paducah, Ky.; Aiken, S.C.; and Portsmouth, Ohio.

Major research and development facilities of the Commission are the 

Atomic Energy Laboratory at Ames, Iowa; the Argonne Cancer Research 

Hospital at Chicago, Ill.; the Argonne 

National Laboratory at Chicago, Ill.; 

the Bettis Atomic Power Laboratory at Pittsburgh, Pa.; the Brookhaven

National Laboratory at Upton, Long 

Island, N.Y.; the Knolls Atomic

Power Laboratory at Schenectady, N.Y.; the Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory at Los Alamos, N. Mex.; the 

Mound Laboratory at Miamisburg, Ohio; the Oak Ridge Institute of Nuclear Studies at Oak Ridge, Tenn.; the

Oak Ridge National Laboratory at 

Oak Ridge, Tenn.; the E. O. Lawrence Radiation Laboratory at Berkeley, Calif., and its extension at Livermore, Calif.; the Research Laboratory, University of Rochester, Rochester,

N.Y.; the Sandia Laboratory at Albuquerque, N. Mex.; the University of 

California Medical Research Facilities,

Los Angeles, Calif.; the National Reactor Testing Station at Idaho Falls, Idaho; and the Nevada Test Site at 

Las Vegas, Nev.

Approved. 

GLENN T. SEABORG, Chairman.

Regulations, Title 14, Chapter II] CREATION AND PURPOSE.-The Civil Aeronautics Act of 1938 (52 Stat. 973; 

49 U.S.C. 401) established a five-mem ber Civil Aeronautics Authority as an independent Federal agency charged with broad responsibilities for the "encouragement and development" of

United States civil aviation, and vested with safety and economic rulemaking and adjudicatory powers. Within the

Authority was an Air Safety Board en trusted with aircraft accident investigation and also the Office of the Ad ministrator of Civil Aeronautics, the 

Authority's executive officer in the field of air safety.

Under Presidential Reorganization Plans III and IV, effective June 30, 

1940, the five-member Authority was renamed the Civil Aeronautics Board. 

The Air Safety Board was abolished and its functions transferred to the 

Civil Aeronautics Board. The Office of the Administrator (Civil Aeronau tics Administration) was transferred to the Department of Commerce.

The Federal Aviation Act of 1958 

(72 Stat. 731), which repealed the

Civil Aeronautics Act of 1938, pro vided for the continuation of the Board as an independent agency. It transferred, however, the safety rulemaking function to the Administrator, Federal Aviation Agency, and required the

Board to determine the "probable cause" of all accidents rather than allow delegation of this function to the Administrator.

The Board exercises its powers independently. Its decisions are not subject to review by any executive department or agency, except for the

ORGANIZATION.-The Civil Aero nautics Board is an independent Federal agency composed of five members appointed for 6-year terms by the President with the consent of the Senate, with no more than three members appointed from the same political party. 

Each year the President designates one member as chairman and another as vice chairman. Reorganization Plan 13 of 1950 provided that executive and administrative functions of the Board be vested in the chairman, subject to certain limitations. Reorganization 

Plan 3 of 1961 authorized the Board to delegate any of its functions to members of the Board or to staff members, subject to approval of two or more Board members. The plan also gave the chairman authority to assign to personnel, including Board members, functions delegated by the Board under the plan. The Board is assisted by a staff of administrative personnel and experts in the field of law, economics, accounting, and air safety.

FUNCTIONS 

In general the Board performs three functions: (1) regulation of the economic aspects of domestic and international United States air carrier operations and of the common carrier operations of foreign air carriers to and from the United States; (2) participation in the establishment and development of international air transporta-

tion; and (3) promotion of safety in civil aviation. These functions are described briefly in the following paragraphs.

ECONOMIC REGULATION.-The Board is responsible for granting authorizations to carriers to engage in interstate and foreign air transportation. It issues permits to foreign air carriers authorizing them to engage in air transportation between the United States and foreign countries, and also authorizes the navigation of foreign civil aircraft in the United States for other purposes.

The Board has jurisdiction over tariffs, and the rates and fares charged the public for air transportation; it establishes rates for the carriage of mail by air carriers; and it authorizes and pays subsidy to certain air carriers where required by the public convenience and necessity. 

In the interest of maintaining competition the Board regulates mergers, acquisitions of control and interlocking relationships involving air carriers, and passes on contracts for cooperative working arrangements between air carriers. The Board also has jurisdiction over unfair competitive practices of air carriers and ticket agents engaged in air transportation or the sale of tickets for this purpose.

The Board regulates the accounting practices of air carriers and requires them to file regular financial and Office

INTERNATIONAL CIVIL AVIATION.- 

The Board consults with and assists the Department of State in the negotiation of agreements with foreign governments for the establishment or development of air routes and services. 

SAFETY ACTIVITIES.-The Board in vestigates accidents involving civil aircraft and holds public hearings to assist in determining the facts, circumstances, and probable causes thereof; it makes such recommendations to the 

Administrator of the Federal Aviation

Agency, as will tend to prevent similar accidents in the future; makes such reports and recommendations public as may be deemed by it to be in the public interest; and conducts special studies and investigations to reduce aircraft accidents and prevent their CL recurrence.

United States gives Congress the power "To exercise exclusive Legislation in all Cases whatsoever, over such District (not exceeding ten Miles square) as may, by Cession of particular States, and the Acceptance of Congress, become the Seat of the Government of the United States. * * *"

In accordance with this provision, Congress, on July 16, 1790 (1 Stat. 

130; 4 U. S. C. 6), and on March 3, 1791, passed acts establishing the District of Columbia.

Until 1846, when Vir ginia's portion, Alexandria City and County, was returned, the District included the corporation of Washington, the corporation of Alexandria, the cor poration of Georgetown, and the counties of Washington and Alexandria. A French engineer, Maj. Pierre 

Charles L'Enfant, planned and partly laid out the new city of Washington, and Maj. Andrew Ellicott continued the work.

In 1802 the first government of the District of Columbia consisted of a mayor, appointed by the President of the United States, and a city council,

EXPORT-IMPORT BANK OF WASHINGTON 

411 lected by the residents. The city counil was given the right in 1812 to elect he mayor of Washington, and in 1820 he election was put in the hands of the eople. In 1871, however, Congress cted to abolish the corporations of Washington and Georgetown and the evy court of Washington County in avor of a territorial form of government.

The new form of administration was omposed of a governor, a board of ublic works, and a legislative assemly consisting of a Council and a House of Delegates. Also, at that time, and until March 4, 1875, the District of Columbia was represented in the lower ouse of Congress by a delegate. The overnor and the members of the oard of public works and of the counil were appointed by the President by and with the advice and consent of the 

Senate. The 22 Members of the House of Delegates and the Delegate to Congress were elected by the people. 

After June 20, 1874, a change was made, and the District was governed by three commissioners appointed by he President. This temporary form of government lasted until July 1, 1878, when the permanent commission government was established. The act of 

Congress of June 11, 1878 (20 Stat. 

Director Director Director 

Executive Vice President 

102), creating the present District government, makes no provision for the franchise. 

ORGANIZATION.-The government of the District is administered by a threeman Board of Commissioners, two of whom, appointed from civilian life by the President, must have been actual residents of Washington for 5 years next before their appointment. These two Commissioners are confirmed by the Senate and serve a 3-year term. 

The President selects from time to time from the Corps of Engineers of the Army the third Commissioner, who must have served at least 15 years in the Corps and have a rank not lower than that of captain.

The District Commissioners, who are also members of the Zoning Commission, have authority over all the usual activities of a municipal government. They prepare annually estimates of the expenditures of the District, which estimates are submitted to Congress through the Bureau of the Budget. Under the Constitution of the 

United States, Congress must pass all legislation affecting the District. Approved.

Farm Credit Administration was es tablished as an independent agency in 

1933 by Executive Order 6084. 

Under Reorganization Plan I, dated 

April 25, 1939, the Farm Credit Administration became a part of the 

Department of Agriculture. How ever, the Farm Credit Act of 1953 again made the Farm Credit Administration an independent agency of the executive branch of the Government. 

PURPOSE. The Farm Credit Ad ministration supervises and coordinates a cooperative credit system for agriculture. This system provides long- and short-term credit to farmers and their cooperative marketing, purchasing, and business service organizations.

MANAGEMENT.-A 13-member Fed eral Farm Credit Board, created by the Farm Credit Act of 1953, is a parttime policy-making body for the Farm 

Credit Administration. Twelve mem bers of the Board, one from each farm credit district, are appointed by the 

President of the United States after

giving consideration to nominations made by Federal land bank associations, production credit associations, and cooperatives borrowing from the banks for cooperatives. The thirteenth member is appointed by the Secretary of Agriculture as his representative. 

The Board selects the Governor of the 

Farm Credit Administration who is the chief executive officer under the Board.

The President of the United States approves the appointment of the Governor as long as there is any Government capital in banks and associations supervised by the Farm Credit 

Administration. 

Each of the three credit servicesland bank, short-term credit, and cooperative bank-is headed by a Director appointed by the Governor. Each of these Directors is also designated as a Deputy Governor. 

All the expenses of the Farm Credit 

Administration, including examination expense, are paid from assessments against the banks and associations it supervises. 

DISTRICT ORGANIZATION. -The 

United States is divided into 12 farm credit districts. In one city in each district are a Federal land bank, a Federal intermediate credit bank, and a bank for cooperatives. Each district also has a part-time policy-making farm credit board of seven members which members are ex-officio directors of each of the three banks in that district. 

Each bank has its own officers.

Board. 

Activities of the three banks in a district are coordinated through the district farm credit board and a president's committee.

The Examination Division of the Farm Credit Administration examines these banks and the local associations.

Federal Land Banks and Federal Land Bank Associations 

The 12 Federal land banks, 1 in each farm credit district, and the local Federal land bank associations, were established under authority of the Fed eral Farm Loan Act of 1916 (39 Stat. 

360; 12 U.S.C. 641), which has been broadened by various amendments. 

OWNERSHIP.-The Federal land bank system is cooperative and is completely farmer-owned. All of the stock of the approximately 717 Federal land bank associations is owned by their member-borrowers. All of the stock of the 12 land banks is owned by the Federal land bank associations.

TYPE OF LOANS.-Farmers obtain ong-term mortgage loans from the and banks through Federal land bank associations. Farmers and ranchers give = first mortgage on their farms or anches as security for such loans and generally agree to repay the loans in annual or semiannual installments. 

Part-time farmers and family-type corporations engaged in farming operations are also eligible to borrow, under certain limitations. 

PURPOSES FOR WHICH LOANS ARE 

MADE.--Farmers and ranchers may ob 

Hain land bank loans for general agricultural purposes and other requirements of the owner of the land mortgaged under rules and regulations of the Farm Credit Administration. 

AMOUNT OF LOAN.-The amount oaned may not exceed 65 percent of the appraised normal agricultural value of the farm offered as security plus any amount of the indebtedness used to pay for related stock. However, the appraisal may, consistent with community values, also reflect home advantages and the availability to a typical operator of the property of earnings from other dependable sources to supplement the normal earning power of the farm. 

INTEREST RATES.-The rate of in terest on loans now being paid is 5.2 percent in 1 district, and 52 percent in 11 districts. It is based on the cost of funds in the investment market plus the cost of operation.

SOURCE OF FUNDS.-Land banks ob tain the money to make loans principally from the sale of consolidated Federal farm loan bonds to the investing public. These bonds are not guaranteed by the Government either as to principal or interest.

The land banks use the notes and mortgages of farmers and stockmen who borrow from them, together with other assets, as collateral for the bonds.

WHERE TO APPLY FOR A LOAN.- 

Farmers needing such credit should apply to the manager of the Federal land bank association in the community in which the farm to be offered as security is located. 

Federal Intermediate Credit Banks 

The 12 Federal intermediate credit banks, 1 in each farm credit district, were authorized by the Agricultural 

Credits Act of 1923 (42 Stat. 1454; 12 

U.S.C. 1021 et seq.).

OWNERSHIP.-Prior to January 1, 

1957, the Federal intermediate credit banks were entirely Governmentowned. Pursuant to the Farm Credit

Act of 1956, production credit associations have acquired $66.0 million of class B stock of the banks, and other financing institutions hold $3.3 million of participation certificates issued by the banks. The 1956 act provides for the gradual retirement of Governmentowned capital stock as private capital and surplus reserves are built up in sufficient amount to support the financial operations of the banks. 

TYPES OF LOANS.-These banks make loans to, and discount agricultural paper for, production credit associations, State and national banks, agricultural credit corporations, livestock loan companies, and similar lending groups; and may make loans to and discount paper for banks for cooperatives and Federal land banks.

The credit banks do not lend directly to farmers and stockmen or otherwise conduct a general banking business.

TIME FOR WHICH LOANS ARE MADE. Ordinarily, the maturities of notes discounted or accepted as security for loans by the intermediate credit banks coincide with the usual time for

the marketing of crops or livestock from which liquidation is expected, usually not more than 12 months.

Under the law such notes, with maturities of not more than 7 years, are eligible for discount or for acceptance as collateral for loans.

DISCOUNT RATE.-The discount or interest rate charged by an intermediate credit bank is determined by the board of directors of the bank with the approval of the Farm Credit Administration. Lenders which rediscount with an intermediate credit bank are not permitted to charge their borrowers on such loans more than 4 percent a year in excess of the discount rate of the credit bank in effect at the time the loan is made, except that a rate of not in excess of 6 percent may be charged when the discount rate of the credit bank is less than 2 percent a year.

SOURCE OF FUNDS.-The banks ob tain the funds they use in their lending operations principally from sales to the investing public of short-term consolidated collateral trust debentures which are the joint and several obligations of the 12 banks. These debentures are not guaranteed by the United States Government, either as to principal or interest.

Production Credit Associations The Farm Credit Act of 1933 (48 

Stat. 257, 259; 12 U. S. C. 1131, 1131d), approved June 16, 1933, authorized the establishment of local production credit associations and 12 production credit corporations, 1 in each farm credit district. When the production credit corporation in each of the 12 farm credit districts was merged with the Federal intermediate credit bank of the district on January 1, 1957, the bank assumed the responsibility for the supervision of the production credit associations.

OWNERSHIP.-The associations were originally capitalized by the Government-owned production credit corporations; however, on January 3, 1966, 468 of the 471 associations had retired all Government capital and were com pletely owned by their farmer-members. The 3 remaining associations are largely owned by farmer-members. 

The Government-owned capital stock, which totaled $580,000 on January 3, 1966, is held by the Governor of the 

Farm Credit Administration. 

All voting stock in a production credit association is owned by its member-borrowers, who elect the directors from their number. Each stockholder has one vote regardless of the number of shares he owns. The directors elect the officers and the executive committee and hire the employees.

TYPE OF LOANS.-Farmers obtain short-term credit for all types of farm and ranch operations from local production credit associations. 

PURPOSES FOR WHICH LOANS ARE MADE. Farmers obtain production credit association loans for general agricultural purposes and other requirements of the borrowers.

SIZE OF LOANS.-The size of each loan depends on the financial require ments of the member's individual farm operations, his ability to use it wisely, and his ability to repay it from his income without danger of impairing the efficiency of his farm operations. Loans are usually made on a budgeted basis for periods up to 1 year. Some loans for capital and semi-capital purposes may be made with maturities up to 

7 years.

INTEREST RATES.-Production credit associations provide credit to members at the lowest possible cost consistent with sound business practices. The rate of interest varies among associations. 

Interest is charged only for the actual number of days each dollar is outstanding.

SOURCE OF FUNDS.-The associa tions do not lend Government funds. 

They obtain most of their loan funds by rediscounting farmers' notes with the Federal intermediate credit banks.

WHERE TO APPLY FOR A LOAN.- 

Farmers needing such credit should ap- 

---

FEDERAL AVIATION AGENCY 

417 ply to their local production credit association or one of its field offices or representatives. 

Banks for Cooperatives

The 12 district banks for cooperatives and the Central Bank for Cooperatives (Washington, D.C.) were organized and chartered by the Governor of the Farm Credit Administration under authority of the Farm Credit Act of 1933 (48 Stat. 257, 261; 12 U.S.C. 

1134, 1134f). The banks for cooperatives were established to provide a permanent source of credit on a sound business basis to farmer cooperatives. 

The Central Bank for Cooperatives serves district banks for cooperatives by making direct loans to them and participating in loans that exceed their respective lending limits. District banks for cooperatives, one located in each of the 12 farm credit districts, serve associations in their areas. 

OWNERSHIP.-Cooperatives own all of the capital stock of two banks. They are increasing their investment in the other banks by purchasing stock in proportion to their current interest payments and through the payment of patronage refunds by the banks in the form of stock. As their investment grows, Government-owned capital will be repaid.

ELIGIBILITY.— -To be eligible to bor row from a bank for cooperatives, a cooperative must be an association in which farmers act together in marketing farm products, purchasing farm supplies, or furnishing farm business services and must meet the requirements set forth in the Farm Credit Act of 1933, as amended. 

TYPES OF LOANS.-Three distinct classes of loans are made to farmer cooperatives commodity, operating capital, and facility loans. 1 

¹ Organization chart on page 626.

INTEREST RATES.-Interest rates are determined by the board of directors of the bank with the approval of the 

Farm Credit Administration. 

Current Activities 

In the year ended December 31, 1965, farmers and their cooperatives borrowed $7 billion from banks and associations operating under supervision of the Farm Credit Administration. 

Farmers and ranchers borrowed $1.2 billion from the cooperative land bank system in 1965, and were using $4.3 billion of land bank mortgage credit on January 1, 1966. Nearly 

368,000 farmers are members of Federal land bank associations. 

Farmers borrowed $4.1 billion from the production credit associations in 

1965. About 544,000 farmers and ranchers are members of these associations. 

Intermediate credit bank discounts of agricultural paper for privately capitalized financing institutions amounted to $296 million in 1965. 

Their discounts for and loans to production credit associations totaled $5 billion.

About 2,900 farmer cooperatives use the credit facilities of the banks for cooperatives. In 1965, farmer cooperatives borrowed $1.3 billion from these banks. Approved.

PROGRAMS SAFETY REGULATION.-The promul gation of safety regulations is provided for under titles III, V, and VI of the act. These include the examination, inspection, certification (including medical), and rating of airmen, and the administration of regulations and surveillance of regulated activities. 

Under these titles the Agency develops regulations for promulgation by the Administrator on all safety matters relating to manufacture, operation, and maintenance of aircraft; performs flight inspection of air navigation facilities in the United States and, as required, abroad; and provides for enforcement of the safety regulations.

It administers air traffic control of civil and military air operations within

Regulations, Title 47, Chapter I] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.- -The Federal Communications Commission was created by the Communications Act of 1934 (48 Stat. 1064; 15 U. S. C. 

21; 47 U. S. C. 35, 151-609), and administers that act, as amended. It also has additional regulatory jurisdiction under the provisions of the Communi cations Satellite Act of 1962 (76 Stat. 

419; 47 U.S.C. 701-744).

PURPOSE.-The Commission created "for the purpose of regulating interstate and foreign commerce in communication by wire and radio so as to make available, so far as possible, to all people of the United States a rapid, efficient, nationwide, and worldwide wire and radio communication service with adequate facilities at reasonable charges, for the purpose of the national defense, for the purpose of promoting safety of life and property through the use of wire and radio communication, and for the purpose of securing a more effective execution of this policy by centralizing authority heretofore granted by law to several agencies and by granting additional authority with respect to interstate and foreign commerce in wire and radio communication." was 

ORGANIZATION.-The Federal Com munications Commission is an independent Federal agency composed of 7 members appointed for 7-year terms by the President with the consent of the Senate, not more than 4 of whom may be members of the same political party. 

The Chairman, designated by the Pres ident, serves as the chief executive of ficer of the Commission, responsible for its executive and administrative functions except those which, because of their program importance, are performed by the 7-man Commission. The substantive functions of the Commission are executed by the Commission, and, by delegations of authority, through a panel of commissioners, individual commissioners, 4 integrated operating bureaus (see Functions and 

Activities), and the following additional staff organizations: 

Office of Executive Director (ex ecutive director), which is directly responsible to the Commission under the supervision of the Chairman, provides administrative leadership and coordination of staff activities in carrying out the policies, programs, and procedures of the Commission through overall supervision and coordination; assists the Chairman in carrying out the administrative and executive responsibilities of the Chairman; and, under the general policy guidance of the Defense Commissioner, directs emergency preparedness functions assigned to the Commission by Executive 

Order 11092 of February 26, 1963, and directs defense coordination and mobilization activities of the Commission. Office of the Chief Engineer, which plans, develops, and directs broad scientific, technical, and specialized engineering programs looking toward the more effective use of radio, television, and wire communications in the public interest; directs the development and coordination of engineering phases of communications regulation including equipment type approval and type acceptance and standardization; directs frequency allocation activities; maintains liaison with the executive branch on frequency management matters; directs certain technical aspects of negotiations on international telecommunications matters; directs operation of the Commission's laboratory and licenses experimental radio stations.

Office of the General Counsel, which functions as chief legal adviser to the Commission and other staff organizations; represents the Commission in litigation, and institutes civil and criminal enforcement proceedings; cooperates with the Common Carrier Bureau and the Office of Chief Engineer on

 ederal Deposit Insurance Corporation was organized under authority of secion 12B of the Federal Reserve Act, pproved June 16, 1933 (48 Stat. 162; 

2 U. S. C. 264). By the act approved eptember 21, 1950 (64 Stat. 873; 12 

J.S.C. 1811-1831), section 12B of he Federal Reserve Act, as amended, as withdrawn as part of the Federal Reserve Act and made a separate inependent law known as the "Federal 

Deposit Insurance Act." The act also nade numerous amendments to the ormer Federal Deposit Insurance law. 

PURPOSE. The chief purpose of the 

Corporation is to insure the deposits of Il banks which are entitled to the enefits of insurance under the law. 

The major functions of the Corporaon are to pay off the depositors of sured banks closed without adequate rovision having been made to pay aims of their depositors, to act as eceiver for all national banks placed receivership and for State banks laced in receivership when appointed eceiver by State authorities, and to revent the continuance or developent of unsafe and unsound banking ractices. In protecting depositors the orporation may also make loans to or urchase assets from the insured banks hen such loans or purchases will ■cilitate a merger or consolidation and ill reduce the probable loss to the 

Corporation. The Corporation is also uthorized to make such loans or purase of assets in order to prevent the osing of an insured bank or to repen a closed insured bank when the orporation considers the continued peration of such bank is essential to rovide adequate banking service in e community.

ORGANIZATION.-Management of the orporation is vested in a board of rectors of three members. The Presient appoints two members, one of hom is elected chairman, for terms 6 years, by and with the advice and nsent of the Senate. The Comptroller 798-477-6628 of the Currency serves ex officio as the third member. The law requires that not more than two members of the board shall belong to the same political party.

FINANCES. No appropriations are made by Congress to the Corporation. 

Its entire income consists of assessments on insured banks and income from investments. As of December 31, 1964, the Corporation's surplus (the Deposit 

Insurance Fund) amounted to approx imately $2,844,665,216.

The annual assessment rate for each insured bank is 1/12 of 1 percent of the assessment base, with assessments payable semiannually calculated at onehalf the annual assessment rate multiplied by the bank's assessment base for the immediately preceeding semiannual period. The assessment base is the average of deposits shown in two reports of condition in each semiannual assessment period, after deductions of 1623 percent of demand deposits and 

1 percent of time and savings deposits.

Each year the insured banks are credited pro rata with 6623 percent of the Corporation's net assessment income. 

The credit is applied toward the payment of assessments due the following July, and any excess credit is applied against subsequent assessments becoming due.

The Corporation is authorized to borrow from the U.S. Treasury, and the Secretary of the Treasury is authorized and directed to loan to the Corporation on such terms as may be fixed by the Corporation and the Secretary, not to exceed $3,000,000,000 outstanding at any one time, when in the judgment of the Board of Directors of the Corporation such funds are required for insurance purposes. No borrowings have been made under this authorization.

NUMBER OF BANKS PARTICIPATING IN DEPOSIT INSURANCE.-In the past 31 

years the number of banks and branches in the United States has been changed principally through mergers and by the growth of branch banking.

At the beginning of 1934 there were approximately 15,000 banks and 3,000 branches in operation. Of these banks, 86 percent were insured by the Fed eral Deposit Insurance Corporation. 

At the close of 1964 there were 14,281 banks and about 15,450 branches, with 97 percent of the incorporated banks of deposit participating in Federal deposit insurance.

Federal Home Loan Bank System CREATION.-The Federal Home oan Bank System was created by uthority of the Federal Home Loan 

Bank Act, approved July 22, 1932 (see itations under Federal Home Loan 

Bank Board), to provide credit reerve for savings and home-financing nstitutions.

CAPITAL AND FUNDS.-The capital stock of the district Federal Home Loan Banks is entirely owned by institutions which have been accepted into membership, each of which is required to purchase stock. As of December 31, 1965, stock owned by member institutions amounted to $1,277,263,345.

The banks may obtain other loanable funds through the issuance of consolidated obligations, through deposits accepted from member institutions and from other Federal Home Loan 

Banks.

ELIGIBLE INSTITUTIONS.—The types of institutions eligible to become mem bers of the Federal Home Loan Banks are savings and loan, building and loan, homestead associations, savings and cooperative banks, and insurance companies. Every Federal savings and loan association is required to become a member of its regional Federal Home Loan Bank, and to qualify for insurance of accounts (see Federal Savings and Loan Insurance Corporation). 

On December 31, 1965, there were 5,053 members in the System, having combined assets of $132,920,000,000, located in the 50 States, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the District of Columbia. 

Through that date the Federal Home Loan Banks had advanced to these member institutions a total of about $37,739,000,000 of which $31,742,- 

000,000 had been repaid, leaving outstanding a balance of $5,007,000,000. POWER TO BORROW.

States. Consolidated obligations amounting to $5,221,000,000 were outstanding on December 31, 1965. In case of need the Secretary of the Treasury is authorized to purchase consol idated Federal Home Loan Bank obligations up to a billion dollars out-

Federal Savings and Loan Associations 

These associations are provided for by section 5 of the Home Owners' Loan Act of 1933 (48 Stat. 132) as amended. They are chartered and supervised by the Federal Home Loan Bank Board, and may be either new institutions or converted from Statechartered institutions upon application. As of December 31, 1965, there were 2,011 Federal savings and loan associations, with combined assets of more than $66,714,956,000.

Federal Savings and Loan Insurance Corporation CREATION.-The Federal Savings and Loan Insurance Corporation was created by title IV of the National 

Housing Act (see citations under Federal Home Loan Bank Board), to insure the safety of savings in thrift and home-financing institutions.

ORGANIZATION.-The operations of the Federal Savings and Loan Insur ance Corporation come under the general direction and supervision of the 

Federal Home Loan Bank Board. 

FUNCTIONS.-The Corporation insures the safety of savings up to $10,000 for each investor's account in an insured institution. All Federal savings and loan associations, and those State-chartered building and loan, savings and loan, homestead associations, and cooperative banks which apply and are approved, are insured. On 

December 31, 1965, there were 4,508 insured institutions, with total assets of about $124,586,000,000.

DEFAULT PROCEDURE.- -To prevent the default of an insured institution or restore it to normal operation, the Corporation may make loans to, purchase assets of, or make a financial contribution to such an institution. In the event of a default by any insured institution, payment of each insured ac- 

count in such insured institution, which is surrendered and transferred to the Corporation, shall be made by the Corporation as soon as possible, either (1) by cash or (2) by making available to each insured member a transferred account in a new insured institution in the same community or in another insured institution in an amount equal to the insured account of such insured member. 

FUNDS.-Income of the Corpora tion consists principally of premiums paid by insured institutions and interest earned on investments. All income above expenses is transferred to reserves. Reserves and unallocated income, as of December 31, 1965, totaled $1,537,000,000. The Corporation is authorized to obtain additional funds for insurance purposes from the 

United States Treasury not exceeding $750,000,000 outstanding at any one time. In addition, insured associations may be required to deposit up to 1 percent of their savings capital with the Corporation. These borrowing and deposit authorities have never been exercised.

RETIREMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK.- 

The capital stock of the Corporation, originally issued in the amount of $100,000,000 and formerly held by the United States Treasury, has now been completely retired. As provided by law, effective June 27, 1950, the Corporation retired at the end of each fiscal year an amount of its capital stock equal to 50 percent of its net income for the year.
